questions.question: How many points does a team get for winning a match?
questions.explanation: Three for a win, one for a draw, nothing for a loss. Add them up and that is the whole league table.
questions.why: Every conversation about the table is a conversation about points. This is the currency.
questions.use: "Ugly win, but three points is three points."

questions.question: How many clubs are in the Premier League?
questions.explanation: Twenty clubs. Each plays the other nineteen twice, home and away, which makes 38 games a season.
questions.why: It tells you how long the season is and why one bad month is not the end of the world.
questions.use: "It's 38 games. One bad month doesn't decide it."

questions.question: How many clubs go down to the Championship at the end of a season?
questions.explanation: The bottom three are relegated and three come up to replace them. Relegation costs a club a fortune and its best players.
questions.why: Come spring, half the league is talking about nothing else.
questions.use: Ask him: "Who do you think goes down this year?" He has a list.

questions.question: How long is a match, before any added time?
questions.explanation: Two halves of 45 minutes. Added time on top makes up for stoppages, so it usually runs closer to 100.
questions.why: So you know when it is actually over, and why "two minutes left" takes ten.
questions.use: "Ninety minutes plus whatever he adds. Could be a while."

questions.question: How many players does each team have on the pitch at kick-off?
questions.explanation: Eleven a side, one of them the goalkeeper. Lose a player to a red card and it is ten men.
questions.why: "Down to ten men" is meaningless unless you know it started at eleven.
questions.use: "Ten men now. They'll sit back and defend."

questions.question: Which colour card means a player is sent off?
questions.explanation: Red means off. Yellow is a warning, and two yellows in one game add up to a red.
questions.why: The sofa reacts to a red card before the commentator does. You want to be in on it.
questions.use: "That's a red. Early bath for him."

questions.question: Which player is allowed to handle the ball inside their own penalty area?
questions.explanation: The goalkeeper, and only inside the box. Step outside it and the same rules apply as for everyone else.
questions.why: Half of all shouting at the telly is about handball. Knowing the one exception makes you sound sure.
questions.use: "Keeper's outside his box, he can't pick that up."

questions.question: How far from goal is a penalty kick taken?
questions.explanation: Twelve yards, straight in front of goal, only the keeper to beat. Around three in four go in.
questions.why: A penalty is the tensest moment in a match and he will want company for it.
questions.use: "Twelve yards, keeper to beat. Don't look at me, I can't watch either."

questions.question: What does VAR stand for?
questions.explanation: Video Assistant Referee: a team in a room checking goals, penalties and red cards on replay while everyone waits.
questions.why: "VAR is checking" happens every single match and stops the room dead. Knowing why buys you the pause.
questions.use: "VAR's checking it. Don't celebrate yet."

questions.question: Since 2022, how many substitutions can a Premier League team make in a match?
questions.explanation: Five, in three separate stoppages plus half-time. It was three for decades before the rule changed in 2022.
questions.why: Substitutions are where he judges the manager. Knowing the limit lets you join the judging.
questions.use: Ask him: "He's used all five already? Bit early for that?"

questions.question: What happens when a league match ends level?
questions.explanation: A draw: one point each. Extra time and penalties only happen in cup games that must have a winner.
questions.why: So you know a league draw is over at the whistle, and a cup draw is just getting started.
questions.use: "It's the league, so that's it. Point each."

questions.question: What is a clean sheet?
questions.explanation: Letting in nothing. The goalkeeper's favourite statistic, and the defence's bragging right.
questions.why: It is the compliment that makes him think you watched the whole match.
questions.use: "Another clean sheet. The defence has been solid."

questions.question: A hat-trick is how many goals by one player in one match?
questions.explanation: Three. Two is a brace. There is no word for four, which tells you how rare it is. The player keeps the match ball.
questions.why: He will say brace and hat-trick without explaining them. Now you do not need him to.
questions.use: "Two already. One more and it's a hat-trick."

questions.question: Which division sits directly below the Premier League?
questions.explanation: The Championship, confusingly named: winning it makes you promoted, not champions of much.
questions.why: "They'll be in the Championship next year" is the insult of choice in spring.
questions.use: Ask him: "Which of the clubs that came up do you think stays up?"

questions.question: How do the three promoted clubs get out of the Championship?
options: Top two plus a play-off winner
questions.explanation: The top two go up automatically. The next four play a mini knockout for the third place; its final is called the richest game in football.
questions.why: Late May, the play-off final is on and he knows someone whose club is in it.
questions.use: "Play-off final. One game for a hundred million pounds."

questions.question: When two teams finish level on points, what usually separates them?
questions.explanation: Goal difference: goals scored minus goals let in. It is why a 4-0 win matters more than a 1-0 win late in a season.
questions.why: Title races and relegation fights come down to it, and it is the bit he loves explaining.
questions.use: "They're level on points, so it's on goal difference. Every goal counts now."

questions.question: When can clubs buy and sell players?
questions.explanation: Two transfer windows: the summer, and the month of January. Outside them, nothing moves, whatever the newspapers say.
questions.why: Transfer rumours are half of what he reads. Knowing when they can actually happen is the filter.
questions.use: "Window's shut. That rumour can't happen until January."

questions.question: How long is each half of extra time in a cup match?
questions.explanation: Two halves of fifteen minutes, played when a cup match is level after ninety. If it is level after that, it is penalties.
questions.why: Cup nights run late. This is how you know exactly how late.
questions.use: "Extra time. Thirty more minutes, then penalties. Put the kettle on."

questions.question: In a penalty shootout, how many kicks does each side take before sudden death?
questions.explanation: Five each, alternating. If it is level after that, one each until somebody misses. England fans have suffered here.
questions.why: The one moment he cannot look at the screen. You can be the one who knows the format.
questions.use: "Five each, then sudden death. Who's taking the fifth?"

questions.question: Which is the oldest cup competition in the world?
questions.explanation: The FA Cup, first played in 1871. Every club in England can enter, so a village team can end up playing Liverpool.
questions.why: January cup weekends are about small clubs beating big ones. That is the whole charm, and now you know why.
questions.use: Ask him: "Any giant-killings this weekend?"

questions.question: What is a match between two local rivals called?
questions.explanation: A derby, pronounced darby. Manchester, Merseyside, North London: same city, decades of grudges.
questions.why: Derby week changes his mood for a fortnight. Naming it correctly is the least you can do.
questions.use: Ask him: "It's the derby this weekend, isn't it? Are you nervous?"

questions.question: Which body runs the Champions League?
questions.explanation: UEFA, European football's governing body. FIFA runs the World Cup. Neither is loved.
questions.why: Midweek European nights are a separate mood. Knowing who runs them is the first step.
questions.use: "UEFA night. Different anthem, different vibe."

questions.question: Over two legs, what decides which team goes through?
questions.explanation: The aggregate: add the two scores together. Win the first leg 2-0 and lose the second 1-0, you go through 2-1 overall.
questions.why: European knockout nights are impossible to follow without this. With it, you are ahead of half the pub.
questions.use: Ask him: "So what's the aggregate? Who's actually ahead?"

questions.question: What is nil in football?
questions.explanation: Zero. A goalless draw is nil-nil, a 2-0 win is two-nil. Football has its own word for nothing.
questions.why: Saying "two-zero" marks you as a newcomer faster than anything else.
questions.use: "Two-nil. Comfortable, that."

questions.question: Which two domestic cup competitions do English clubs enter?
options: The FA Cup and the Champions League
The FA Cup and the Europa League
The League Cup and the play-offs
The FA Cup and the League Cup
questions.explanation: The FA Cup and the League Cup (Carabao Cup). Both are knockouts run alongside the league; the European competitions are separate again.
questions.why: He will switch between three competitions in a single week and assume you know which is which.
questions.use: Ask him: "Is this the league or one of the cups?"

questions.question: What happens to a team that loses a cup match?
options: They are out of that competition
They play a replay next week
questions.explanation: Cups are knockouts: lose once and that competition is finished for the season. In the league a defeat costs points and you carry on.
questions.why: It explains why a cup defeat lands harder than a league one, even against a small club.
questions.use: "That's them out, then. No second chance in the cup."

questions.question: What is Wembley?
questions.explanation: England's national stadium, in north London. Both domestic cup finals are played there, along with the FA Cup semi-finals and England's home games.
questions.why: "A trip to Wembley" is how fans describe a cup run that has gone deep, and it comes up every spring.
questions.use: Ask him: "Have you ever been to a game at Wembley?"

questions.question: Why do big clubs often pick a weaker side in the early League Cup rounds?
options: It is a rule of the competition
To rest players for bigger games
questions.explanation: Rotation. With league games and European nights stacked up, a manager rests his first-choice players and hands the young ones a game instead.
questions.why: It stops a weak line-up looking like a disaster and gets you into the argument about priorities.
questions.use: "He's rotated for this. The league game at the weekend is the priority."

questions.question: Which is Europe's third club competition, below the Europa League?
questions.explanation: The Conference League, played on Thursday nights like the Europa League. Smaller trophy, same format, and a European away day either way.
questions.why: European nights come in three varieties and he will not say which one he means.
questions.use: Ask him: "Is that the Europa League or the Conference League?"

questions.question: In a two-legged cup round, where is the second leg played?
options: At the same ground as the first
questions.explanation: One match at each ground, so both sides get a home game. The two scores are added together and the aggregate decides who goes through.
questions.why: European knockout nights make no sense until you know that both matches count as one.
questions.use: "Second leg at home. They just need to keep it tight."

questions.question: Alan Shearer retired in 2006 with how many Premier League goals?
questions.explanation: 260, for Blackburn and Newcastle. Nobody had passed it by 2024, and he has been on Match of the Day ever since.
questions.why: His name comes up every time a striker scores a lot. Now you know why he is the yardstick.
questions.use: "Nobody's near Shearer's 260, are they? Kane didn't get there."

questions.question: Thierry Henry is a legend at which club?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, where he scored 228 goals and has a statue outside the ground. Elegant, quick, French, and adored.
questions.why: He is the player Arsenal fans of a certain age measure everyone against.
questions.use: Ask him: "Henry or Bergkamp, who was better?" Then sit back.

questions.question: Who managed Manchester United from 1986 to 2013?
questions.explanation: Sir Alex Ferguson: thirteen league titles, two Champions Leagues, and a stand named after him. Every manager since is compared to him.
questions.why: Half of football's phrases are his: Fergie time, the hairdryer, squeaky bum time.
questions.use: "Nobody's matched Ferguson's thirteen titles. Nobody's going to."

questions.question: Who scored the injury-time goal that won Manchester City the title in 2012?
questions.explanation: Sergio Agüero, in the 94th minute of the final game, against QPR, to snatch the title from United on goal difference. The commentary is just 'Agüerooo'.
questions.why: It is the moment fans use to explain why football is worth the stress.
questions.use: "Agüerooo. That's why people put themselves through this."

questions.question: Steven Gerrard spent almost his whole career at which club?
questions.explanation: Liverpool, 1998 to 2015, as captain. He dragged them to the 2005 Champions League from 3-0 down. Then he became a manager, less happily.
questions.why: The one-club captain is a type he admires. Gerrard is the template.
questions.use: "Gerrard was Liverpool. You don't get one-club players like that now."

questions.question: Which Frenchman managed Arsenal from 1996 to 2018?
questions.explanation: Arsène Wenger. Three titles, the unbeaten 2003-04 season, and he changed how English clubs ate and trained. Fans sing his name to this day.
questions.why: Wenger is the reason Arsenal fans talk about football as an art form.
questions.use: Ask him: "Was Wenger a genius or did he stay too long?" Both answers are strongly held.

questions.question: Frank Lampard scored 211 goals for which club, more than any striker in its history?
questions.explanation: Chelsea, over thirteen years. Two hundred and eleven goals from midfield is absurd; strikers would take it.
questions.why: He is the answer to "which midfielder scored like a striker", a debate he has had.
questions.use: "Lampard got 211 for Chelsea from midfield. From midfield."

questions.question: Harry Kane passed Jimmy Greaves in 2023 to become the top scorer in the history of which club?
questions.explanation: Tottenham. Kane then left for Bayern Munich, chasing the trophies he had not won at Spurs.
questions.why: Kane is the polite, decent superstar every fan respects, even rivals.
questions.use: Ask him: "Was Kane right to leave Spurs for Bayern?"

questions.question: Peter Schmeichel kept goal for which club in the 1990s?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, five league titles, a huge Dane in a green jersey. His son Kasper won the league with Leicester in 2016.
questions.why: Father and son both won the league. That is the fun fact, and it is yours.
questions.use: "Schmeichel and his son both won the league. Different clubs, twenty years apart."

questions.question: Eric Cantona kicked a fan in 1995 while playing for which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, at Crystal Palace. He was banned for eight months, then came back and won the double. Collar up, always.
questions.why: Cantona is the reference for any moody genius footballer. Now you get the reference.
questions.use: "Bit of a Cantona moment, that." (When a player loses his temper spectacularly.)

questions.question: Which Welsh winger won thirteen league titles with Manchester United?
questions.explanation: Ryan Giggs, one club for his whole career, 1991 to 2014. Thirteen titles with one team.
questions.why: He is the standard for loyalty and longevity. Any long-serving player gets compared to him.
questions.use: "Giggs won thirteen titles at one club. Twenty-three years."

questions.question: Gianfranco Zola, a Chelsea favourite of the late 1990s, came from which country?
questions.explanation: Italy. Small, brilliant, and voted Chelsea's greatest ever player by fans in 2003, before the money arrived.
questions.why: Older Chelsea fans light up at his name. It is a kindness to know it.
questions.use: Ask him: "Did you ever see Zola play? Everyone says he was magic."

questions.question: Roy Keane, the fierce captain known as Keano, led which club in the 1990s and 2000s?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, and Ireland. Terrifying midfielder, now a pundit who is terrifying to other pundits.
questions.why: He is on TV every week saying something brutal. Knowing his history explains the tone.
questions.use: "Roy Keane wouldn't have stood for that." (When a player looks like he isn't trying.)

questions.question: Which Liverpool forward is nicknamed the Egyptian King?
questions.explanation: Mohamed Salah, who joined from Roma in 2017 and scored 32 league goals in his first season, a new high for a 38-game campaign at the time.
questions.why: The song fans sing about him is one he will know all the words to.
questions.use: Ask him: "Is Salah the best signing Liverpool ever made?"

questions.question: Didier Drogba scored the winning penalty in the 2012 Champions League final for which club?
questions.explanation: Chelsea, in Bayern Munich's own stadium. He had also scored the late equaliser. The man for the big occasion, and he knew it.
questions.why: "Big-game player" is a phrase he uses. Drogba is who he means.
questions.use: "He's a bit of a Drogba. Only turns up for the big ones."

questions.question: Wayne Rooney's overhead kick in the 2011 Manchester derby was scored for which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United. Voted the best goal in the first twenty years of the Premier League. He started at Everton and ended as United's top scorer.
questions.why: It is the goal that gets replayed whenever anyone scores an overhead kick.
questions.use: "Rooney against City. That's the overhead kick everyone means."

questions.question: Who captained Manchester City to their first Premier League title in 2012?
questions.explanation: Vincent Kompany, the Belgian centre-back with a statue outside the Etihad. He later became a manager and won the Bundesliga with Bayern.
questions.why: Kompany is the answer when City fans get misty about the club before the trophies were routine.
questions.use: Ask him: "Kompany or Rodri, who mattered more to City?"

questions.question: Who scored a hat-trick in under three minutes for Southampton in 2015?
questions.explanation: Sadio Mané, 2 minutes 56 seconds against Aston Villa. He later won everything at Liverpool alongside Salah.
questions.why: The fastest-hat-trick pub question. Having the answer ready is pure impress.
questions.use: "Mané did a hat-trick in under three minutes once. Under three minutes."

questions.question: Who managed Leicester City to the 2016 Premier League title?
questions.explanation: Claudio Ranieri, the Italian nobody expected anything from. Leicester had started the season as 5000-1 outsiders. Sacked nine months later.
questions.why: Leicester 2016 is the fairy tale every small club fan mentions. It is the proof that it can happen.
questions.use: "Leicester won it at 5000-1. Anything can happen." (When his team are underdogs.)

questions.question: Robin van Persie left Arsenal in 2012 to join which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, where he won the title in his first season. Arsenal fans consider it a betrayal, United fans a masterstroke.
questions.why: Players leaving for rivals is the sorest subject in football. This is the classic case.
questions.use: Ask him: "Worst betrayal in football: Van Persie or Sol Campbell?"

questions.question: Which Belgian midfielder was Manchester City's playmaker for a decade from 2015?
questions.explanation: Kevin De Bruyne: passes nobody else saw, six league titles, and Chelsea let him go for almost nothing first.
questions.why: He is the modern example of a playmaker, the word you will hear in every tactical chat.
questions.use: "De Bruyne saw passes nobody else did. That's what a playmaker is."

questions.question: David Beckham scored from the halfway line in 1996 playing for which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, against Wimbledon, on the opening day of the season. It made him famous overnight. Then came Posh.
questions.why: Beckham is the crossover celebrity; this goal is where it started.
questions.use: "That's where Beckham started. Halfway line, first game of the season, 1996."

questions.question: The North London derby is between Arsenal and which club?
questions.explanation: Tottenham. Four miles apart, and the grudge dates to 1913, when Arsenal moved north into Spurs' patch uninvited.
questions.why: If he supports either club, this fixture decides his mood for a fortnight.
questions.use: Ask him: "Do you actually know why Arsenal and Spurs hate each other?" Plenty of fans don't.

questions.question: Which two clubs play the Merseyside derby?
questions.explanation: Liverpool and Everton, whose grounds were a short walk apart across a park. Families in the city are split down the middle.
questions.why: It is called the friendly derby because relatives sit together. It has more red cards than any other fixture.
questions.use: "The friendly derby, and it's had more red cards than any other. Bit ironic."

questions.question: The Manchester derby is City against whom?
questions.explanation: Manchester United. City spent decades in United's shadow; United fans called them the noisy neighbours. The noise has got louder.
questions.why: The derby is a status contest as much as a match. Knowing the history explains the heat.
questions.use: "Noisy neighbours. That's what Ferguson called City."

questions.question: Which two clubs contest the M23 derby?
questions.explanation: Brighton and Crystal Palace, forty miles apart along the M23. It began as a feud between two managers in the 1970s and simply carried on.
questions.why: Nobody outside the two clubs understands it, so knowing about it marks you as someone who pays attention.
questions.use: Ask him: "Why do Brighton and Palace hate each other? They're miles apart."

questions.question: The Tyne-Wear derby is Newcastle against which club?
questions.explanation: Sunderland. Two rivers, twelve miles, and well over a century of mutual dislike. When both are in the Premier League, the region stops.
questions.why: It is the fixture northern fans mention when southerners talk about derbies.
questions.use: "Tyne-Wear derby. That one's properly nasty."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Gunners?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, founded by workers at the Royal Arsenal munitions factory in 1886. Hence the cannon on the badge.
questions.why: Nicknames come up in every match: the Gunners, the Reds, the Blues. This one has the best story.
questions.use: "They're the Gunners because the club started at a weapons factory. Hence the cannon."

questions.question: Which club is known as the Toffees?
questions.explanation: Everton, after a toffee shop near the ground. Before home games a woman in old-fashioned dress throws sweets into the crowd, to this day.
questions.why: The Toffee Lady is the kind of detail that makes a fan grin. It is yours now.
questions.use: "Everton have a Toffee Lady who throws sweets to the crowd. That's why they're the Toffees."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Magpies?
questions.explanation: Newcastle, for the black and white stripes. The fans are the Toon Army, and they are loud.
questions.why: "The Toon" is what he will call Newcastle without explaining. Now it needs no explaining.
questions.use: "The Toon are at home. St James' will be bouncing."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Cherries?
questions.explanation: Bournemouth, for the cherry-red shirts and the cherry orchards that stood near the old ground.
questions.why: A small club with a smaller ground and a nice story. Good to have when they come up in conversation.
questions.use: "The Cherries. Tiny ground, about eleven thousand."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Bees?
questions.explanation: Brentford, in west London. The badge is a bee, the fans chant 'buzz', and the club runs on statistics rather than money.
questions.why: Brentford are the club clever fans admire. Knowing them is a signal.
questions.use: "Brentford scrapped their academy and built a team on data. And it worked."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Seagulls?
questions.explanation: Brighton. The name started as a chant to wind up Crystal Palace fans, who sing 'Eagles'. Rivalry gave them their identity.
questions.why: Two seaside birds, one grudge. It is a good line and it is true.
questions.use: "Brighton only became the Seagulls to annoy Palace. Eagles versus Seagulls."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Villans?
questions.explanation: Aston Villa, spelt with an a. One of the oldest clubs in England, founder members of the Football League in 1888, and European champions in 1982.
questions.why: Villa fans feel undervalued. Knowing they won the European Cup is the way to their heart.
questions.use: "Villa won the European Cup in 1982. People forget that."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Cottagers?
questions.explanation: Fulham, whose ground, Craven Cottage, has an actual cottage in one corner. London's oldest professional club, from 1879.
questions.why: The prettiest ground in London, on the Thames. Good for a day out, good for a line.
questions.use: "Craven Cottage. There's an actual cottage in the corner of the ground."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Black Cats?
questions.explanation: Sunderland. A black cat was the club's lucky mascot at a cup final in 1937, and fans voted the name official in 2000.
questions.why: Sunderland fans are famously loyal through misery. The Netflix series about them is the reference.
questions.use: Ask him: "Did you watch Sunderland 'Til I Die? Was it as painful as it looked?"

questions.question: Which club plays in claret and blue and has Birmingham City as its city rival?
questions.explanation: Aston Villa. West Ham and Burnley borrowed the claret and blue from Villa. The Birmingham fixture is the Second City derby.
questions.why: Three clubs, one colour scheme. He may not know who had it first.
questions.use: Ask him: "Who had claret and blue first, Villa or West Ham?" It was Villa.

questions.question: Which two clubs contest the East Anglian derby?
questions.explanation: Ipswich Town and Norwich City, forty miles apart. Fans joke it is the Old Farm derby, a pun on Glasgow's Old Firm.
questions.why: The pun alone is worth knowing. It always gets a laugh from the right crowd.
questions.use: "The Old Farm derby. Ipswich and Norwich. It's a farming joke."

questions.question: Leeds United's rivalry with Manchester United is known as what?
questions.explanation: The Roses rivalry: Yorkshire's white rose against Lancashire's red, from a war fought five hundred years before football existed.
questions.why: It is the one derby with a medieval origin story. Perfect impress material.
questions.use: "Leeds and United is the Roses rivalry. It goes back to an actual war in the 1400s."

questions.question: Who are Chelsea's nearest neighbours in the Premier League?
questions.explanation: Fulham. Stamford Bridge and Craven Cottage are under two miles apart, both in the same borough.
questions.why: West London derbies are lower-key, and he wants them won all the same.
questions.use: "Chelsea and Fulham are basically neighbours. Two miles apart."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Sky Blues?
questions.explanation: Coventry City. A 1960s manager, Jimmy Hill, changed the kit to sky blue and wrote the fans' song to go with it.
questions.why: Coventry are the romantic story: a big-city club that fell to the fourth tier and climbed all the way back.
questions.use: "Coventry were in the fourth division in 2018. Now look at them."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Tractor Boys?
questions.explanation: Ipswich Town, from Suffolk farming country. Rival fans meant it as an insult; Ipswich fans adopted it and put it on scarves.
questions.why: The best nicknames were insults first. This is a good example to have ready.
questions.use: "Tractor Boys started as an insult from other fans. Ipswich just took it."

questions.question: Which club is nicknamed the Eagles?
questions.explanation: Crystal Palace, in south London. For years a real bald eagle called Kayla flew round the ground before matches.
questions.why: A live eagle at a football match is a fact people do not believe. Enjoy telling it.
questions.use: "Palace used to have an actual eagle flying round the pitch before games."

questions.question: Which club's fans sing You'll Never Walk Alone before every home game?
questions.explanation: Liverpool, since the 1960s. It is a show tune from a musical, and the words are over the gates at Anfield.
questions.why: It is the one football song everyone has heard. Knowing whose it is matters.
questions.use: "You'll Never Walk Alone. Every Liverpool game, scarves up. Gets me every time."

questions.question: Which club plays at the Emirates Stadium?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, since 2006. Before that they played at Highbury, a few hundred yards away, which is now flats with the pitch as a garden.
questions.why: "At the Emirates" is how he will say Arsenal are at home. It also has a fun afterlife story.
questions.use: "Highbury's flats now. The old pitch is the communal garden."

questions.question: Anfield is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Liverpool. It was Everton's ground first, until a rent row in 1892 sent Everton across the park and left the landlord to start Liverpool.
questions.why: Liverpool only exist because of a landlord dispute. That is a genuinely good story.
questions.use: "Liverpool were founded because Everton fell out with their landlord over rent."

questions.question: Old Trafford is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, since 1910. Bobby Charlton called it the Theatre of Dreams and the name stuck.
questions.why: The nickname turns up in every United broadcast. Knowing who coined it is the extra step.
questions.use: "Theatre of Dreams. Bobby Charlton's line, wasn't it?"

questions.question: Stamford Bridge is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Chelsea. The stadium existed before the club: it was built in 1877 and Chelsea were founded in 1905 to fill it, in a pub over the road.
questions.why: A club invented to fill an empty stadium is the kind of fact that flips a conversation.
questions.use: "Chelsea were founded in a pub to fill a stadium that was already there."

questions.question: Which club's badge shows a cockerel standing on a football?
questions.explanation: Spurs. The cockerel has been on the badge and the roof since 1909, and it wears spurs on its legs, which is the pun.
questions.why: He has looked at that badge a thousand times without noticing the spurs. You can be the one who did.
questions.use: Ask him: "Have you noticed the cockerel on the Spurs badge is wearing spurs?"

questions.question: Which club's badge features the liver bird?
questions.explanation: Liverpool. The liver bird is the city's symbol, a cormorant holding seaweed in its beak, on the town hall and the badge.
questions.why: Badge stories are how you show you looked properly.
questions.use: "That's the liver bird. It's on the buildings all over the city too."

questions.question: Villa Park is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Aston Villa, since 1897. The huge stand behind one goal is the Holte End, and the ground has hosted more FA Cup semi-finals than any other.
questions.why: Villa Park is a ground fans of every club have visited for a semi-final. He will have a memory of it.
questions.use: Ask him: "Have you ever been to Villa Park? Everyone seems to have a semi-final story."

questions.question: Goodison Park was for over a century the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Everton, from 1892 until they moved to a new stadium on the docks in 2025. Goodison was the first purpose-built football ground in England.
questions.why: Grounds closing is an emotional subject. Knowing this one shows you understand why.
questions.use: Ask him: "Did you ever go to Goodison before they left? People say it was special."

questions.question: St James' Park is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Newcastle. Right in the city centre; you can see the stands from the shops. Fans in the top tier are famously far from the pitch.
questions.why: It is the ground people mean when they say a stadium is part of the city.
questions.use: "St James' is right in the middle of town. You can walk from the shops."

questions.question: Which club's badge shows a red devil holding a trident?
questions.explanation: Manchester United. Matt Busby borrowed the Red Devils name from a Salford rugby team in the 1960s, and the devil joined the badge in 1970.
questions.why: Even United fans rarely know the devil came from rugby. That is the point of knowing it.
questions.use: "The Red Devils name came from a rugby league team in Salford. Busby nicked it."

questions.question: Which club has a cannon on its badge?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, for the Royal Arsenal weapons works in Woolwich where the club began. The cannon has pointed in different directions over the years.
questions.why: Badge, nickname and origin story all in one. Efficient.
questions.use: "Cannon on the badge, Gunners as the nickname. It all comes from the weapons factory."

questions.question: Which club's badge is a bee?
questions.explanation: Brentford. Red and white stripes and a bee, for the Bees. Their old ground, Griffin Park, had a pub on every corner.
questions.why: Four pubs, four corners is a fact he may already love. If not, he will now.
questions.use: "Brentford's old ground had a pub on every corner. All four."

questions.question: Which club's badge shows an eagle perched on a football?
questions.explanation: Crystal Palace. Below the eagle is a drawing of the actual Crystal Palace, the giant glass exhibition hall the club is named after. It burned down in 1936.
questions.why: The club is named after a building that no longer exists. Good to know why.
questions.use: "Palace are named after a glass palace that burned down in 1936. It's on the badge."

questions.question: Craven Cottage is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Fulham, on the bank of the Thames. There is a real cottage in one corner, and the stand finished in 2024 has a rooftop swimming pool.
questions.why: A stadium with a swimming pool is a fact worth having.
questions.use: "Fulham's new stand has a rooftop pool. At a football ground."

questions.question: The City Ground is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Nottingham Forest, on the River Trent. Notts County's ground is three hundred yards away across the water, the closest two grounds in England.
questions.why: Two league grounds you can see from each other. Nobody expects that fact.
questions.use: "Forest and Notts County's grounds are 300 yards apart. You can see one from the other."

questions.question: Which club plays at the Stadium of Light?
questions.explanation: Sunderland, since 1997. It was built on a coal mine, and the name honours the miners' lamps. Benfica's ground in Lisbon has the same name.
questions.why: Two Stadiums of Light is a decent pub question, and the coal mine is the better half of the answer.
questions.use: "The Stadium of Light's built on an old coal mine. The name's for the miners' lamps."

questions.question: Elland Road is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Leeds United, since 1919. Known for being loud and hostile to visiting teams, which Leeds fans consider a compliment.
questions.why: "Elland Road on a night game" is a phrase he will use with feeling.
questions.use: "Elland Road under the lights. Proper hostile."

questions.question: Which club plays at the smallest ground in Premier League history, holding about 11,000?
questions.explanation: Bournemouth, at the Vitality Stadium, also called Dean Court. Some Championship grounds are three times the size.
questions.why: Ground size is a bragging point. Knowing the smallest gives you a comparison for everything.
questions.use: "Bournemouth's ground holds eleven thousand. That's smaller than some rugby clubs."

questions.question: Which club plays at the ground known as the Amex?
questions.explanation: Brighton, at Falmer on the edge of the Downs. It took fourteen years of planning fights to build; before that they played on an athletics track.
questions.why: Brighton's rise from homeless to European football is a story fans respect.
questions.use: "Brighton played on an athletics track for twelve years before the Amex. Now they're in Europe."

questions.question: Which club's badge shows a ship above three diagonal stripes for the city's rivers?
questions.explanation: Manchester City. The ship is for the Ship Canal and the city's trade, the stripes for its three rivers, and the red rose is for Lancashire.
questions.why: Reading a badge like a map is a small party trick. This is the best badge for it.
questions.use: "City's badge is a map: the ship's the canal, the stripes are the three rivers."

questions.question: Portman Road is the home of which club?
questions.explanation: Ipswich Town, since 1884, their home for the club's entire history. Two managers who went on to run England have statues outside.
questions.why: Ipswich are a small club with a big history. The statues are the proof.
questions.use: "Two England managers came from Ipswich. Ramsey and Robson, both have statues outside."

questions.question: Which club's badge features a tree?
questions.explanation: Nottingham Forest. A tree above wavy lines for the River Trent, designed by a fan in a competition in 1973.
questions.why: Forest are the club with two European Cups and a badge drawn by a supporter. Both are worth knowing.
questions.use: "Forest's badge was designed by a fan in a competition. And they've won two European Cups."

questions.question: In which year was Arsenal founded?
questions.explanation: 1886, by workers at the Royal Arsenal munitions factory in Woolwich, south-east London. That is where the cannon on the badge and the Gunners nickname come from.
questions.why: The badge, the nickname and the origin are one story. Knowing it makes the whole club make sense.
questions.use: "Arsenal started as a works team at a weapons factory. Hence the cannon."

questions.question: In which part of London did Arsenal begin life?
questions.explanation: Woolwich, south of the river. In 1913 they moved north to Highbury, a few miles from Tottenham, uninvited. Spurs fans consider it the original sin of the derby.
questions.why: This is the root of the Arsenal–Spurs hatred, and plenty of fans only half know it.
questions.use: Ask him: "Do you know why Spurs actually hate Arsenal? It's about a house move."

questions.question: Where did Arsenal play before the Emirates Stadium?
questions.explanation: Highbury, from 1913 to 2006, with its art deco stands. The old ground is flats now, and the pitch is the residents' garden.
questions.why: Older Arsenal fans say Highbury with feeling. The flats detail is the bit they enjoy.
questions.use: "Highbury's flats now, isn't it? The pitch is the garden."

questions.question: What is Arsenal's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Gunners, for the armaments works. The fans call themselves Gooners.
questions.why: Gooner is the word he uses for himself. Gunners is the word for the team. Mixing them up is noticed.
questions.use: "Come on you Gunners." (The chant. Sung before every match.)

questions.question: What colour are Arsenal's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Red body and white sleeves, since 1933. Before that, plain dark red. The change was Herbert Chapman's, the manager who made Arsenal a big club in the 1930s.
questions.why: The white sleeves are the club's signature. Knowing they were a manager's idea is a good extra.
questions.use: "The white sleeves were a manager's idea in 1933. Before that they were plain red."

questions.question: Which manager gave Arsenal the white sleeves and got the local Tube station renamed after the club?
questions.explanation: Herbert Chapman, manager 1925 to 1934: two titles, an FA Cup, and ideas like floodlights and numbered shirts. In 1932 he got Gillespie Road station renamed Arsenal.
questions.why: He is why there is a statue of a man in a suit outside the Emirates, and why the Tube stop says Arsenal.
questions.use: Ask him: "Do you know why the Tube station is called Arsenal? A manager talked them into it."

questions.question: In which season did Arsenal go the whole league campaign without losing?
questions.explanation: 2003-04: 38 games, 26 wins, 12 draws, no defeats. The team is called the Invincibles, and no English club has matched it since.
questions.why: He will bring it up unprompted. Now you can bring it up first.
questions.use: "The Invincibles season. Thirty-eight games without losing."

questions.question: Who managed the Invincibles?
questions.explanation: Arsène Wenger, in charge 1996 to 2018, the longest-serving manager in the club's history. He changed English football's diet and training. Fans sing his name to this day.
questions.why: Wenger divides Arsenal fans: genius, or stayed too long. It is a conversation he has had many times.
questions.use: Ask him: "Was Wenger a genius, or did he stay about five years too long?"

questions.question: Who captained the Invincibles?
questions.explanation: Patrick Vieira, the tall French midfielder who ran the team. He later became a manager himself.
questions.why: Vieira is who he means by a proper midfielder. Every Arsenal midfielder since gets compared to him.
questions.use: "They've not had a midfielder like Vieira since." (Any time the midfield looks soft.)

questions.question: Who is Arsenal's top scorer in the club's history?
questions.explanation: Thierry Henry, 228 goals across two spells, 1999 to 2007 and a short return in 2012. His statue outside the Emirates shows him sliding on his knees.
questions.why: Henry is the club's modern hero. If you know one Arsenal player, know him.
questions.use: Ask him: "Did you ever see Henry play live?" If yes, sit back for ten minutes.

questions.question: How many league titles had Arsenal won by the end of the 2025-26 season?
questions.explanation: Fourteen, the 2025-26 title being the fourteenth. Thirteen of them came before 2004; then a long wait.
questions.why: The number he will quote against Liverpool and United fans. Have it ready.
questions.use: "Fourteen titles. They finally added one after twenty-two years."

questions.question: How many times had Arsenal won the FA Cup by 2020?
questions.explanation: Fourteen, the 2020 win over Chelsea being the fourteenth. No club had won it more often at that point.
questions.why: The FA Cup is Arsenal's speciality. It is the trophy fans of other clubs mock them for loving.
questions.use: "Arsenal and the FA Cup. Fourteen of them by 2020."

questions.question: Who are Arsenal's biggest rivals?
questions.explanation: Tottenham, four miles up the road. The North London derby; two a season, and they decide his mood for a fortnight each.
questions.why: Knowing the rival is the minimum. Knowing derby week is coming is the bonus.
questions.use: Ask him: "When's the derby? Do I need to clear the diary?"

questions.question: In which year did Arsenal move to the Emirates Stadium?
questions.explanation: 2006. The stadium cost so much that the club went nine years without a trophy while paying for it. Fans called it the banter era.
questions.why: The trophy drought explains a decade of jokes at Arsenal's expense. He remembers every one.
questions.use: Ask him: "Was the Emirates worth nine years without a trophy?"

questions.question: Which final did Arsenal reach in Paris in 2006, losing 2-1 to Barcelona?
questions.explanation: The Champions League final. Their goalkeeper was sent off after eighteen minutes, they led anyway, and lost to two late goals. Arsenal fans have not forgiven the referee.
questions.why: European finals are rare for Arsenal, so each one is a story he can tell in detail.
questions.use: Ask him: "Paris 2006. Was Lehmann's red card the end of it, or would they have lost anyway?"

questions.question: Tony Adams captained Arsenal to league titles in how many different decades?
questions.explanation: Three: 1989 and 1991, 1998, and 2002. A centre-back who played for Arsenal for his entire career and has a statue outside the ground.
questions.why: Mr Arsenal, fans call him. Three decades as captain is the fact to have.
questions.use: "Adams captained them to titles in three different decades. Nobody else in England has done that."

questions.question: Who managed Arsenal to the league titles of 1989 and 1991?
questions.explanation: George Graham, an ex-Arsenal player whose teams defended first and won 1-0 a lot. Rivals sang 'boring, boring Arsenal'; Arsenal fans answered 'one-nil to the Arsenal'.
questions.why: 'Boring Arsenal' was the taunt for a decade, and the club's identity before Wenger arrived.
questions.use: "'One-nil to the Arsenal' was a real chant. They won a lot of games that way under Graham."

questions.question: What is the name of Arsenal's dinosaur mascot?
questions.explanation: Gunnersaurus Rex, designed by a young fan in 1993. The club made him redundant in 2020 to save money and reinstated him after an outcry led by a player.
questions.why: The mascot being sacked and un-sacked is a story that gets a laugh every time.
questions.use: "They sacked Gunnersaurus in 2020 and had to bring him back. Fans revolted."

questions.question: Which Arsenal striker with a statue outside the Emirates played in the Invincibles team?
questions.explanation: Thierry Henry. Bergkamp has a statue too, but he retired in 2006. Henry scored 30 league goals in the unbeaten season.
questions.why: Two statues, one question he will enjoy: which of them was better.
questions.use: Ask him: "Henry or Bergkamp?" Then just listen.

questions.question: In which season did Arsenal win the league title for the first time in twenty-two years?
questions.explanation: 2025-26, with 85 points, after finishing second three years in a row. The previous title was the Invincibles' in 2003-04.
questions.why: It is the freshest happy memory he has. Asking about it is a gift.
questions.use: Ask him: "Where were you when they finally won it?"

questions.question: What is Aston Villa's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Villa Park, since 1897, in the Aston area of Birmingham. The stand behind one goal, the Holte End, is one of the biggest single stands in England.
questions.why: 'The Holte End' is a phrase he will use. Now you know it is a stand, not a person.
questions.use: "The Holte End's loud today."

questions.question: What colours do Aston Villa play in?
questions.explanation: Claret and blue. Villa had it first; West Ham and Burnley copied it. A common quiz argument.
questions.why: Three clubs share the colours and Villa fans want credit for being first.
questions.use: Ask him: "Who had claret and blue first, Villa or West Ham?" He will say Villa, and he is right.

questions.question: In which year was Aston Villa founded?
questions.explanation: 1874, by members of a chapel cricket team looking for something to do in winter. One of England's oldest clubs.
questions.why: Villa fans feel the club's history is undervalued. Knowing its age is a way in.
questions.use: "Villa are one of the oldest clubs in the country. 1874."

questions.question: Aston Villa were founder members of which competition in 1888?
questions.explanation: The Football League, the first league anywhere in the world. A Villa director, William McGregor, wrote the letter that proposed it.
questions.why: The league itself was a Villa man's idea. That is a genuinely impressive fact.
questions.use: "A Villa director invented the Football League. Literally wrote the letter proposing it."

questions.question: In which year did Aston Villa win the European Cup?
questions.explanation: 1982, beating Bayern Munich 1-0 in Rotterdam. The European Cup is what the Champions League used to be called.
questions.why: People forget Villa are European champions. Villa fans do not, and love being reminded.
questions.use: "Villa are European champions. 1982, beat Bayern. People always forget."

questions.question: Who scored the winning goal in the 1982 European Cup final?
questions.explanation: Peter Withe, off his shin, from a Tony Morley cross. The word 'Withe' is painted on the goalpost at Villa Park at the exact spot the ball went in.
questions.why: The goalpost detail is the kind of thing only proper fans know.
questions.use: "The scorer's name is painted on the goalpost at Villa Park where the ball went in."

questions.question: How many English league titles has Aston Villa won?
questions.explanation: Seven, six of them before 1911 and the seventh in 1981. For a spell around 1900 they were the biggest club in England.
questions.why: It is the number that explains why Villa fans think of themselves as a big club.
questions.use: "Seven league titles. They were the Manchester United of the 1890s."

questions.question: Who managed Aston Villa to the league title in 1981?
questions.explanation: Ron Saunders, a strict manager who used just fourteen players all season. He quit months before the European Cup win, so his assistant lifted it.
questions.why: Fourteen players for a whole season is a fact that stops modern fans in their tracks.
questions.use: "They won the 1981 title using fourteen players. Fourteen, all season."

questions.question: Who are Aston Villa's city rivals?
questions.explanation: Birmingham City. The Second City derby, played only when the two are in the same division. To Villa fans, 'the Blues' means Birmingham, not Chelsea.
questions.why: If he says 'the Blues' with contempt, this is who he means.
questions.use: "Second City derby. Villa fans think they're the bigger club, and they usually are."

questions.question: What is Aston Villa's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Villans, spelt with an a. Rival fans prefer the other spelling.
questions.why: Spelling it right in a text is a small win.
questions.use: "Come on you Villans." (With an a. He will notice.)

questions.question: Which animal is on the Aston Villa badge?
questions.explanation: A lion, taken from the Scottish royal standard because an early chairman was Scottish. The motto underneath is Prepared.
questions.why: Badge stories are the easiest way to show you looked properly.
questions.use: "The lion on the badge is Scottish. An early chairman brought it with him."

questions.question: Jack Grealish left Aston Villa in 2021 to join which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester City, for £100 million, a British record at the time. He was Villa's captain and a local boy, which made it hurt.
questions.why: The local hero who left for money is a Villa sore point and a good conversation.
questions.use: Ask him: "Do Villa fans forgive Grealish, or is he a traitor for life?"

questions.question: After relegation in 2016, in which year did Villa return to the Premier League?
questions.explanation: 2019, beating Derby in the play-off final at Wembley. Three seasons in the Championship for a club that considers itself a giant.
questions.why: The Championship years are the low point he measures everything against.
questions.use: Ask him: "How bad were the Championship years? Did you keep going?"

questions.question: Which Villa goalkeeper won the World Cup with Argentina in 2022?
questions.explanation: Emiliano Martínez, who also won the award for best goalkeeper at the tournament and celebrated it in a way that upset a lot of people.
questions.why: A World Cup winner between the posts is a bragging right few clubs have.
questions.use: "Villa's keeper won the World Cup. Not many clubs can say that."

questions.question: In which competition did Aston Villa play in 2024-25 for the first time in over forty years?
questions.explanation: The Champions League, after finishing fourth in 2024 under Unai Emery. Their previous appearance in Europe's top competition was 1982-83, defending their European Cup.
questions.why: Villa in the Champions League was the feel-good story of 2024. He will remember the anthem at Villa Park.
questions.use: Ask him: "What was it like hearing the Champions League anthem at Villa Park again?"

questions.question: Which striker left Villa for Manchester United in 1998 and won the treble the next year?
questions.explanation: Dwight Yorke, from Trinidad and Tobago, always smiling. Villa fans watched him win everything the season after he left.
questions.why: Selling your best player and watching him win the treble is a specific kind of pain. It explains a lot.
questions.use: "Villa sold Yorke and he won the treble the next year. Typical."

questions.question: Villa beat Manchester United in the 1994 League Cup final under which manager?
questions.explanation: Ron Atkinson, who had managed United himself. The win stopped United doing a domestic treble that year, which Villa fans enjoy more than the cup.
questions.why: Stopping a rival's treble is worth more than a trophy to some fans. This is the example.
questions.use: "Villa stopped United's treble in 1994. Fans bring it up to this day."

questions.question: Aston Villa are from which city?
questions.explanation: Birmingham. Aston is a district north of the city centre; the ground is next to the motorway.
questions.why: England's second city has two clubs and Villa fans are clear about which is the big one.
questions.use: "Villa's the big club in Birmingham. Ask a Blues fan and duck."

questions.question: The Holte End is a famous stand at which ground?
questions.explanation: Villa Park. It holds around 13,000 and is where the noise comes from. Named after a local landowner's hall.
questions.why: A stand with a name is a stand with a reputation. This one has both.
questions.use: "The Holte End. Thirteen thousand people behind one goal."

questions.question: Which Spanish manager took Villa from the relegation zone in 2022 to the Champions League by 2024?
questions.explanation: Unai Emery, who had won the Europa League four times elsewhere. Villa were 17th when he arrived and fourth eighteen months later.
questions.why: The Emery turnaround is why Villa fans have been so cheerful lately.
questions.use: "Emery took them from the relegation zone to the Champions League in eighteen months."

questions.question: What is Bournemouth's home ground called?
questions.explanation: The Vitality Stadium, also known by its old name, Dean Court. It holds about 11,000, the smallest ground in Premier League history.
questions.why: The tiny ground is the first thing anyone mentions about Bournemouth. Get there first.
questions.use: "Eleven thousand. You could fit their whole crowd in a corner of Old Trafford."

questions.question: What is Bournemouth's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Cherries, for the cherry-red shirts and the cherry orchards that used to stand near the ground.
questions.why: Nicknames turn up in every commentary. This one has a pleasant story.
questions.use: "The Cherries. There were orchards by the old ground."

questions.question: What colours are Bournemouth's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Red and black stripes, copied from AC Milan in the early 1970s because the manager admired them.
questions.why: A small English club in Milan's colours is a neat fact for a match on telly.
questions.use: "Bournemouth's stripes are copied from AC Milan. A manager just liked the look."

questions.question: In which year did Bournemouth first reach the Premier League?
questions.explanation: 2015, for the first time in 116 years of existence. Seven years earlier they had nearly gone out of business.
questions.why: The rise is the whole Bournemouth story. Everything else is footnotes.
questions.use: "First time in the top flight in 2015, after 116 years. Mad."

questions.question: Which manager took Bournemouth from the fourth tier to the Premier League?
questions.explanation: Eddie Howe, a former Bournemouth defender who became manager at 31. Two spells, three promotions, then Newcastle.
questions.why: Howe is the name Bournemouth fans say with love, and Newcastle fans now say too.
questions.use: Ask him: "Is Eddie Howe the best thing that ever happened to Bournemouth?"

questions.question: In which year did Bournemouth go into administration and nearly cease to exist?
questions.explanation: 2008. They started the next season on minus 17 points as a punishment and stayed up anyway. Seven years later they were in the Premier League.
questions.why: From nearly dead to the Premier League in seven years. It is the fact that explains the club.
questions.use: "Bournemouth started 2008-09 on minus seventeen points and were in the Premier League seven years later."

questions.question: Bournemouth is in which English county?
questions.explanation: Dorset, on the south coast: beaches, pine trees, retirees, and one small football ground.
questions.why: Placing a club on the map is the basic courtesy of a conversation.
questions.use: "Bournemouth, down in Dorset. Best beaches of any away day."

questions.question: How many seasons did Bournemouth's first Premier League spell last?
questions.explanation: Five, from 2015 to 2020, when they were relegated on the final day. Two seasons later they were back.
questions.why: Yo-yo clubs are a type. Knowing the pattern lets you predict the conversation.
questions.use: Ask him: "Are they a proper Premier League club now, or a yo-yo club at heart?"

questions.question: After relegation in 2020, in which year did Bournemouth return to the Premier League?
questions.explanation: 2022, finishing second in the Championship under Scott Parker, who was sacked four games into the new season.
questions.why: Sacking the manager who got you promoted is a football classic. This is a clean example.
questions.use: "They sacked the manager who got them promoted after four games. Four."

questions.question: Bournemouth is on which coast of England?
questions.explanation: The south coast, between Southampton and Poole. A seaside town before it was a football town.
questions.why: Geography first. The rest follows.
questions.use: "South coast club. Southampton are the neighbours they don't like."

questions.question: What does Bournemouth's badge show?
questions.explanation: A player heading the ball, in profile, on the red and black stripes. It was drawn in the 1970s and has barely changed.
questions.why: Badge spotting is a low-stakes way to show attention.
questions.use: "Their badge is a bloke heading a ball. Nice and literal."

questions.question: Who are Bournemouth's south-coast rivals?
questions.explanation: Southampton, thirty miles east. Historically the bigger club by far, which Bournemouth fans enjoy pointing out has changed.
questions.why: Rivalries are where fans get funny. This one has a recent role reversal.
questions.use: Ask him: "Are Bournemouth bigger than Southampton now? Be honest."

questions.question: Which striker left Bournemouth for Newcastle in 2020?
questions.explanation: Callum Wilson, their top scorer in the Premier League years, sold after relegation. He kept scoring at Newcastle.
questions.why: Losing your striker after relegation is the price of going down. Wilson is the example.
questions.use: "They had to sell Wilson when they went down. That's what relegation costs."

questions.question: Andoni Iraola, appointed Bournemouth manager in 2023, comes from which country?
questions.explanation: Spain, from the Basque Country. He had made Rayo Vallecano in Madrid play thrilling football on no money, and did the same at Bournemouth.
questions.why: Iraola made Bournemouth a team neutral fans watched on purpose. That is rare for a small club.
questions.use: Ask him: "Did Iraola's Bournemouth actually play the best football in the league for a while?"

questions.question: After leaving Bournemouth in 2020, which club did Eddie Howe go on to manage?
questions.explanation: Newcastle, from 2021. He took them into the Champions League and won their first domestic trophy in seventy years, the 2025 League Cup.
questions.why: Bournemouth's manager becoming a Newcastle hero is a shared story between two sets of fans.
questions.use: "Howe won Newcastle a trophy after seventy years. Bournemouth fans were chuffed for him."

questions.question: What does AFC stand for in AFC Bournemouth?
questions.explanation: Athletic Football Club. The letters were moved to the front in 1971 so the club would appear at the top of alphabetical lists.
questions.why: The alphabetical trick is a perfect pub fact: small, true and slightly ridiculous.
questions.use: "They put AFC at the front so they'd be first in alphabetical lists. That's the whole reason."

questions.question: What was Bournemouth called before 1971?
questions.explanation: Bournemouth & Boscombe Athletic. Boscombe is the suburb where the ground is; locals call the ground Dean Court to this day.
questions.why: Old names come up on old shirts and old photos. He may not know this one himself.
questions.use: Ask him: "Did you know they used to be Bournemouth and Boscombe Athletic?"

questions.question: In which division were Bournemouth playing in 2009, six years before reaching the Premier League?
questions.explanation: League Two, the fourth tier, and fighting relegation from it. Six years later they were playing Manchester United.
questions.why: Fourth tier to top tier in six years is the fastest climb in modern English football.
questions.use: "Fourth division in 2009, Premier League in 2015. Six years."

questions.question: Bournemouth's first ever Premier League season, 2015-16, ended in which position?
questions.explanation: Sixteenth, comfortably safe. Everyone had tipped them to go straight back down. Eddie Howe's team played passing football and stayed up.
questions.why: Staying up in year one is the achievement small clubs are judged on. Bournemouth passed.
questions.use: "Everyone said they'd go straight back down in 2016. Finished sixteenth, easy."

questions.question: Where does the name Dean Court, Bournemouth's ground, come from?
questions.explanation: The Cooper-Dean family, local landowners who gave the club the land in 1910. The stadium sponsor changes; the fans' name for the place does not.
questions.why: Fans use the old name, sponsors use the new one. Knowing both is knowing the club.
questions.use: "Dean Court, or the Vitality if you're the sponsor. Fans say Dean Court."

questions.question: What is Brentford's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Bees. The badge is a bee, the fans chant 'buzz' at throw-ins, and the mascot is called Buzz Bee.
questions.why: It is the friendliest nickname in the league and it comes with a chant.
questions.use: "The Bees. Listen, the fans buzz at throw-ins."

questions.question: What is Brentford's home ground called?
questions.explanation: The Gtech Community Stadium, by Kew Bridge, since 2020. Squeezed between railway lines on the Thames.
questions.why: New grounds lose the old names slowly. He may say Griffin Park by habit.
questions.use: "They're at the Gtech now. Right by Kew Bridge."

questions.question: What was the name of Brentford's old ground, famous for having a pub on every corner?
questions.explanation: Griffin Park, home from 1904 to 2020. Four corners, four pubs. Away fans planned their day around it.
questions.why: The four pubs are the fact every fan knows and loves. It works every time.
questions.use: "Griffin Park had a pub on all four corners. Best away day in the country."

questions.question: In which year were Brentford promoted to the Premier League?
questions.explanation: 2021, beating Swansea 2-0 in the play-off final at Wembley, after losing the final the year before.
questions.why: Losing a play-off final then winning the next one is a story with a happy ending. He will tell it if asked.
questions.use: Ask him: "Were you at Wembley in 2021? After losing the year before?"

questions.question: What colours are Brentford's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Red and white stripes with black shorts. Easy to confuse with Sunderland on a small screen.
questions.why: Kit recognition is how you follow a match without the commentary.
questions.use: "Red and white stripes, black shorts. That's Brentford, not Sunderland."

questions.question: Which Danish manager took Brentford into the Premier League and kept them there?
questions.explanation: Thomas Frank, in charge from 2018 to 2025, seven years, then off to Tottenham. Calm, funny, and adored in west London.
questions.why: Frank was the model of a small-club manager. His move to Spurs is a talking point in itself.
questions.use: Ask him: "Was Thomas Frank right to leave for Spurs?"

questions.question: Brentford's owner made his fortune in what?
questions.explanation: Sports betting. Matthew Benham, a lifelong fan, built a gambling company on statistics and ran the club the same way. He also owns Midtjylland in Denmark.
questions.why: The maths club is Brentford's identity. Knowing why is knowing them.
questions.use: "Brentford's owner is a professional gambler. The whole club runs on his statistics."

questions.question: Brentford is in which part of London?
questions.explanation: West London, near Kew Gardens, wedged between Fulham and QPR. A small corner of a big city.
questions.why: London has a dozen clubs. Placing them is the first skill.
questions.use: "West London. Fulham and QPR are the neighbours."

questions.question: When Brentford went up in 2021, how many years had passed since their previous top-flight season?
questions.explanation: Seventy-four years. Their previous top-flight season was 1946-47, just after the war.
questions.why: Seventy-four years of waiting puts every other club's complaints in perspective.
questions.use: "Brentford waited seventy-four years to get back to the top flight. Since 1947."

questions.question: Ivan Toney left Brentford in 2024 to play in which country?
questions.explanation: Saudi Arabia, joining Al-Ahli for around £40 million. He had been their top scorer for four seasons and served a betting ban in 2023.
questions.why: Players leaving for Saudi money is a live debate. Toney is a name he will bring up.
questions.use: Ask him: "Can you blame Toney for taking the Saudi money?"

questions.question: Who are Brentford's nearest rivals?
questions.explanation: Fulham and Queens Park Rangers, a couple of miles away in west London. Low-key as derbies go, and he wants them won all the same.
questions.why: Small derbies matter as much to the fans in them as the big ones do.
questions.use: "West London derby. Nobody else cares, everyone in Brentford does."

questions.question: What is on the Brentford badge?
questions.explanation: A bee, in a red and white roundel. The griffin from the old ground's name appears on older badges.
questions.why: One badge, one insect. Simple to remember, and the buzz chant follows from it.
questions.use: "Bee on the badge, buzz from the crowd. Consistent, at least."

questions.question: In 2016 Brentford closed their youth academy and replaced it with what?
questions.explanation: A B team, for players released by bigger clubs aged 17 to 20. Cheaper than an academy, and several of them made the first team.
questions.why: Brentford doing things differently is their whole appeal to football hipsters.
questions.use: "Brentford shut their academy and signed rejects from other clubs instead. It worked."

questions.question: Brentford's first ever Premier League match in 2021 was a 2-0 home win over which club?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, on the opening Friday night of the season, live on television. A perfect way to arrive.
questions.why: First-night wins get retold forever. This one was against a giant.
questions.use: "Their first ever Premier League game was beating Arsenal. Friday night, on telly."

questions.question: Christian Eriksen joined Brentford in 2022 after collapsing on the pitch at which tournament?
questions.explanation: Euro 2020, played in 2021, where his heart stopped during a Denmark match. Fitted with a defibrillator, he returned to football at Brentford six months later.
questions.why: Eriksen's comeback is one of the truly moving football stories of the decade, and Brentford made it possible.
questions.use: "Eriksen came back from a cardiac arrest at Brentford. The whole league was cheering him."

questions.question: Brentford's stadium sits next to which London landmark?
questions.explanation: Kew Bridge, over the Thames, a walk from the botanical gardens. The stadium is wedged between two railway lines.
questions.why: Knowing where the ground is turns a fixture into a day out.
questions.use: "It's right by Kew Gardens. Football and a walk round the gardens."

questions.question: At which stadium did Brentford win the 2021 play-off final?
questions.explanation: Wembley, in front of a crowd limited by the pandemic. Their first promotion to the top flight in the club's history under that name.
questions.why: Play-off finals are the happiest and saddest day in a fan's year. This one was the happy kind.
questions.use: Ask him: "What was Wembley like with only ten thousand in?"

questions.question: In which year was Brentford founded?
questions.explanation: 1889, by members of a rowing club looking for a winter sport. They voted between football and rugby, and football won by a few votes.
questions.why: A club that nearly became a rugby team is a fact worth having.
questions.use: "Brentford voted on whether to play football or rugby in 1889. Football won narrowly."

questions.question: Thomas Frank left Brentford in 2025 to manage which club?
questions.explanation: Tottenham. In the same summer Brentford lost their manager, their captain and their top scorer, and were expected to collapse.
questions.why: The summer of 2025 is the moment Brentford fans feared the project was over.
questions.use: Ask him: "Did you think Brentford were finished when Frank, the captain and the striker all left?"

questions.question: Brentford's mascot is called what?
questions.explanation: Buzz Bee. Not a complicated club when it comes to naming things.
questions.why: Mascots are small talk gold when the match is dull.
questions.use: "Buzz Bee. They didn't overthink that one."

questions.question: What is Brighton's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Seagulls. It started in the 1970s as a chant to answer Crystal Palace fans singing 'Eagles', and became the official nickname.
questions.why: A nickname invented to annoy a rival is the best kind. And it explains the Palace thing.
questions.use: "Brighton only became the Seagulls to wind up Palace fans. Seagulls versus Eagles."

questions.question: What is Brighton's home ground commonly called?
questions.explanation: The Amex, after the sponsor, at Falmer on the edge of the South Downs. Officially the American Express Stadium.
questions.why: "At the Amex" is how every Brighton home game is described.
questions.use: "They're at the Amex. Lovely ground, middle of nowhere."

questions.question: Who are Brighton's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Crystal Palace, forty miles away in south London. The M23 derby, named after the motorway between them. Nobody outside the two clubs quite gets it.
questions.why: It is the rivalry that makes no geographical sense, so knowing about it marks you as informed.
questions.use: Ask him: "Why do Brighton and Palace hate each other? They're forty miles apart."

questions.question: In which year were Brighton promoted to the Premier League for the first time?
questions.explanation: 2017, after thirty-four years out of the top flight, under Chris Hughton. Twenty years earlier they had nearly dropped out of the league altogether.
questions.why: The 2017 promotion is the moment the modern club began. He will have a memory of it.
questions.use: Ask him: "Where were you when they went up in 2017?"

questions.question: What colours are Brighton's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Blue and white stripes, with white shorts. Easy to spot, easy to confuse with Sheffield Wednesday.
questions.why: Kit recognition is the fastest way to follow a match.
questions.use: "Blue and white stripes. That's Brighton."

questions.question: Brighton's owner, Tony Bloom, made his money how?
questions.explanation: Professional gambling and a betting-data company. A lifelong fan known at the poker table as the Lizard, he uses his data to find players nobody else has spotted.
questions.why: Brighton's whole business model — buy cheap, sell for a fortune — comes from this one man.
questions.use: "Brighton's owner is a poker player. His data company finds the players before anyone else."

questions.question: Which Italian manager took Brighton into European football for the first time?
questions.explanation: Roberto De Zerbi, who took them to sixth in 2023 and the Europa League, playing football neutral fans tuned in for.
questions.why: De Zerbi's Brighton is the team neutral fans fell for. He is now at Spurs, so the name lives on.
questions.use: Ask him: "Was De Zerbi's Brighton the best football you've seen from a small club?"

questions.question: Which ground did Brighton lose in 1997, leaving them homeless for two years?
questions.explanation: The Goldstone Ground, sold by the owners to developers. Brighton played home games seventy miles away in Gillingham for two seasons while fans fought to save the club.
questions.why: The Goldstone is the trauma every Brighton fan over forty carries. Knowing it shows respect.
questions.use: Ask him: "Did you go through the Goldstone years? Playing home games in Gillingham?"

questions.question: Brighton reached the FA Cup final in 1983 and lost the replay to which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, 4-0 in a replay after a 2-2 draw. Gordon Smith could have won the first game late on. 'And Smith must score,' said the commentator. He didn't.
questions.why: 'And Smith must score' is a Brighton fanzine title and a phrase fans use for any big miss.
questions.use: "'And Smith must score' comes from Brighton's 1983 cup final. He didn't. There's a fanzine named after it."

questions.question: Graham Potter left Brighton in 2022 to manage which club?
questions.explanation: Chelsea, who paid Brighton over £20 million for him. He was sacked within seven months, and Brighton got better without him.
questions.why: Managers leaving for big clubs and flopping is a genre. This is the textbook case.
questions.use: "Chelsea paid twenty million for Potter and sacked him in seven months. Brighton just carried on."

questions.question: Brighton sold Moisés Caicedo to Chelsea in 2023 for roughly how much?
questions.explanation: About £115 million, a British record at the time, for a player they had bought for around £4 million from Ecuador two years earlier.
questions.why: Buy for four, sell for a hundred and fifteen. That is the Brighton model in one transfer.
questions.use: "Brighton bought Caicedo for four million and sold him for a hundred and fifteen. In two years."

questions.question: Brighton is in which county?
questions.explanation: Sussex, on the south coast, an hour from London. The ground is on the edge of the South Downs, next to a university.
questions.why: The seaside city with a football club: useful context for the away-day chat.
questions.use: "Brighton. Sussex, seaside, students and a football club on the Downs."

questions.question: Which Brighton midfielder moved to Liverpool in 2023, months after winning the World Cup?
questions.explanation: Alexis Mac Allister, a World Cup winner with Argentina in December 2022 while a Brighton player. Sold to Liverpool for about £35 million.
questions.why: A World Cup winner in a Brighton shirt is a fact that surprises people.
questions.use: "Brighton had a World Cup winner in their team. Mac Allister, before Liverpool bought him."

questions.question: In which competition did Brighton play their first European campaign, in 2023-24?
questions.explanation: The Europa League. They beat Ajax and Marseille and went out to Roma in the round of sixteen. A club that had been homeless twenty-five years earlier.
questions.why: From Gillingham to Amsterdam in one lifetime is the arc Brighton fans live for.
questions.use: "Brighton beat Ajax in Europe. Twenty-five years after nearly going out of business."

questions.question: Where did Brighton play their home games between 1999 and 2011?
questions.explanation: Withdean, a converted athletics track with temporary stands and a running track between the fans and the pitch. Fans called it the Theatre of Trees.
questions.why: Twelve years on an athletics track then European nights. The contrast is the story.
questions.use: "They played on an athletics track for twelve years. Fans called it the Theatre of Trees."

questions.question: The Brighton v Crystal Palace rivalry takes its name from what?
questions.explanation: The M23 motorway between the two. The actual origin was a feud between two managers in the 1970s, Alan Mullery and Terry Venables, that the fans adopted and kept.
questions.why: A derby caused by two managers falling out is a better story than geography.
questions.use: "The Brighton–Palace thing started because the two managers hated each other in the seventies."

questions.question: In which year was Brighton & Hove Albion founded?
questions.explanation: 1901, replacing a club called Brighton United that had gone bust. Albion is an old poetic name for Britain.
questions.why: The 'Albion' in the name puzzles people. Now you can explain it.
questions.use: "Albion just means Britain. It's the old poetic name."

questions.question: What is Brighton's mascot called?
questions.explanation: Gully, a seagull, with a companion called Gully's Girl. Named after the bird, obviously.
questions.why: Mascot names are a safe question when the match is dull.
questions.use: "Gully. And there's a Gully's Girl."

questions.question: In which year did Brighton's Amex Stadium open?
questions.explanation: 2011, after a fourteen-year fight for planning permission that went to a public inquiry twice. The first league game there was a 2-1 win over Doncaster.
questions.why: Fourteen years to build a ground. Fans remember every planning meeting.
questions.use: Ask him: "Fourteen years to get the Amex built. Did you ever think it wouldn't happen?"

questions.question: Which Brighton manager left in 2024 and was later appointed at Tottenham?
questions.explanation: Roberto De Zerbi, who went to Marseille first. His replacement at Brighton, Fabian Hürzeler, was 31, the youngest manager in Premier League history at the time.
questions.why: Brighton appointing a 31-year-old is the kind of bold move that makes fans of other clubs jealous.
questions.use: "Brighton hired a 31-year-old manager. Younger than some of the players."

questions.question: What is Chelsea's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Stamford Bridge, in Fulham, not Chelsea. The ground was built in 1877 for athletics; the football club was founded in 1905 to fill it.
