questions.why: Three statues outside the ground; knowing all three names is the full set.
questions.use: "Silva, Agüero, Kompany. The three statues. That's the team that started it."

questions.question: In which year did Manchester City beat Manchester United 6-1 at Old Trafford?
questions.explanation: 2011, on the way to their first title. Balotelli scored and lifted his shirt to reveal the words 'Why always me?'
questions.why: 6-1 at Old Trafford is the scoreline City fans bring to every derby argument.
questions.use: "Six-one at Old Trafford. 'Why always me?' That whole day was ridiculous."

questions.question: What is Manchester City's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Citizens, or the Sky Blues. Fans just say City. Cityzens, with a z, is what the club calls its members.
questions.why: Nicknames are how fans refer to their own. Get this one right and he notices.
questions.use: "City. Nobody actually says the Citizens."

questions.question: The Etihad Stadium is on which side of Manchester?
questions.explanation: East Manchester, in a once-industrial area rebuilt around the stadium, the training campus and, more recently, an arena.
questions.why: Knowing where the ground is turns a match into a day out.
questions.use: "It's in east Manchester. They've basically rebuilt the whole area around it."

questions.question: Which Chilean manager won the Premier League with Manchester City in 2014?
questions.explanation: Manuel Pellegrini, the first manager from outside Europe to win the Premier League. Quiet, polite, and replaced by Guardiola two years later.
questions.why: The manager between Mancini and Guardiola is the one everyone forgets. Remembering him is the trick.
questions.use: "Pellegrini won City a title in 2014 and nobody ever mentions him. First non-European to win it."

questions.question: In which year did Manchester City win their first league title?
questions.explanation: 1937. They were relegated the very next season while scoring more goals than anyone in the division. 'Typical City', fans said for decades.
questions.why: 'Typical City' is what older fans say about any self-inflicted disaster. This is where it comes from.
questions.use: "City won the league in 1937 and got relegated the next year. That's where 'typical City' comes from."

questions.question: What is Manchester United's home ground called?
questions.explanation: Old Trafford, since 1910. Bobby Charlton called it the Theatre of Dreams and the name stuck. It holds around 74,000.
questions.why: The Theatre of Dreams is a phrase he uses. Knowing who coined it is the extra step.
questions.use: "Theatre of Dreams. That was Bobby Charlton's line."

questions.question: What is Manchester United's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Red Devils. Matt Busby borrowed the name from Salford's rugby league team in the 1960s because he thought it sounded fiercer than the Busby Babes.
questions.why: The devil came from rugby. Even United fans often don't know.
questions.use: "The Red Devils name was nicked from a Salford rugby team. Busby thought it sounded scarier."

questions.question: Manchester United were founded in 1878 under what name?
questions.explanation: Newton Heath LYR, a railway workers' team in green and gold. They nearly went bust in 1902 and were rescued by a brewer, who renamed them Manchester United.
questions.why: A railway team saved by a brewer: the origin story is better than the badge suggests.
questions.use: "United started as a railway workers' team called Newton Heath. Played in green and gold."

questions.question: Who managed Manchester United from 1986 to 2013?
questions.explanation: Sir Alex Ferguson: thirteen league titles, two Champions Leagues, a stand named after him, and every football phrase from Fergie time to the hairdryer.
questions.why: Ferguson is the yardstick for every manager since. Twenty-seven years, one club.
questions.use: "Thirteen titles under Ferguson. Nobody's getting near that."

questions.question: In which year did Manchester United win the treble of league, FA Cup and Champions League?
questions.explanation: 1999, sealed with two goals in the final three minutes of the Champions League final against Bayern Munich in Barcelona. The first English club to do the treble.
questions.why: '99 is the year United fans return to. It is the peak of everything.
questions.use: Ask him: "Where were you for the final three minutes of the 1999 final?"

questions.question: Which two substitutes scored the late goals in the 1999 Champions League final?
questions.explanation: Teddy Sheringham and Ole Gunnar Solskjær, both off the bench, in the 91st and 93rd minutes. Ferguson said afterwards: 'Football, bloody hell.'
questions.why: 'Football, bloody hell' is a quote he will know. This is where it comes from.
questions.use: "Two subs scored in stoppage time to win the treble. 'Football, bloody hell,' Ferguson said."

questions.question: In which year did the Munich air disaster claim the lives of eight Manchester United players?
questions.explanation: 1958, flying home from a European Cup game, when the plane crashed on take-off in snow. Busby survived and rebuilt the team. A clock at Old Trafford shows that time.
questions.why: Munich is sacred to United. Knowing it, quietly, matters more than any trophy fact.
questions.use: "The Munich clock outside the ground is stopped at the moment of the crash. 1958."

questions.question: Manchester United became the first English club to win the European Cup in which year?
questions.explanation: 1968, beating Benfica 4-1 at Wembley, ten years after Munich. Bobby Charlton, a survivor of the crash, scored twice.
questions.why: The European Cup a decade after the crash, with a survivor scoring, is the story that makes grown men cry.
questions.use: "Ten years after Munich they won the European Cup, and a survivor of the crash scored twice in the final."

questions.question: Which group of United academy players from the early 1990s is known as the Class of '92?
options: Beckham, Scholes, Giggs and the Nevilles
questions.explanation: Beckham, Scholes, Giggs, Butt and the Neville brothers, who won the 1992 FA Youth Cup together and then the treble. A pundit said you win nothing with kids.
questions.why: 'You'll win nothing with kids' is the quote he will produce. Now you know the punchline.
questions.use: "'You'll win nothing with kids.' Alan Hansen said that about the Class of '92. Then they won everything."

questions.question: Who is Manchester United's top scorer in the club's history?
questions.explanation: Wayne Rooney, 253 goals, passing Bobby Charlton's 249 in 2017. He arrived from Everton as an eighteen-year-old in 2004.
questions.why: Rooney overtaking Charlton is the modern-versus-legend debate in one fact.
questions.use: Ask him: "Rooney or Charlton, who was the better United player?"

questions.question: Who are Manchester United's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Liverpool, thirty miles away, the two clubs who have won more than anyone else in England. City is the local derby; Liverpool is the real one.
questions.why: United fans rank their hatreds. Liverpool is top, and it is not close.
questions.use: "City's the neighbours. Liverpool's the enemy. Different things."

questions.question: Cristiano Ronaldo first joined Manchester United in 2003 from which club?
questions.explanation: Sporting Lisbon, aged eighteen, after tormenting United's defenders in a friendly. The players asked Ferguson to sign him on the plane home. He got the number seven.
questions.why: Ronaldo's arrival is a story United fans tell like a legend. It also explains the number seven.
questions.use: "United's players asked Ferguson to sign Ronaldo on the flight home after he ran rings round them in a friendly."

questions.question: How many Premier League titles has Manchester United won?
questions.explanation: Thirteen, all under Ferguson, between 1993 and 2013. Twenty league titles in total, counting the ones before the Premier League.
questions.why: Thirteen and twenty are the two numbers he will quote. Know which is which.
questions.use: "Thirteen Premier Leagues, twenty titles in all. All the recent ones were Ferguson."

questions.question: What was Ole Gunnar Solskjær's nickname as a player?
questions.explanation: The baby-faced assassin: innocent looks, ruthless finishing, often off the bench. He once scored four in twelve minutes as a sub. Later, less happily, the manager.
questions.why: 'Super sub' is a role. Solskjær is the man the phrase was built for.
questions.use: "He's a Solskjær. Comes off the bench and scores." (About any good substitute.)

questions.question: Which manager rebuilt United after the war and after Munich, and has a statue at Old Trafford?
questions.explanation: Sir Matt Busby, manager 1945 to 1969: built the Busby Babes, lost them at Munich, built again and won the European Cup in 1968. The road outside is Sir Matt Busby Way.
questions.why: Busby is the father of the club. Ferguson is the son. Both have statues.
questions.use: "Busby built the club twice. Before Munich and after it."

questions.question: In which year did Manchester United win the Premier League for the thirteenth time?
questions.explanation: 2013, Ferguson's final season. He retired as champion, and the years since have been a long argument about whose fault it is.
questions.why: The post-Ferguson years are the sore subject. Knowing where they start helps you tread carefully.
questions.use: Ask him: "Whose fault is it that United haven't won the league since Ferguson left?"

questions.question: What is the name of the stand at Old Trafford where the loudest United fans gather?
questions.explanation: The Stretford End, at the west end of the ground, named after the district behind it. Where the songs start.
questions.why: Stands with names are stands with reputations. This is United's.
questions.use: "The Stretford End. That's where the noise comes from."

questions.question: Which American family bought Manchester United in 2005?
questions.explanation: The Glazer family, owners of an American football team, who bought the club with borrowed money and loaded the debt onto it. Fans have protested for twenty years.
questions.why: Ask any United fan about the Glazers and stand back. It is the one thing they all agree on.
questions.use: Ask him: "Are the Glazers as bad as everyone says, or is that just an excuse?"

questions.question: Which British billionaire bought a stake in United in 2024 and took over the football side?
questions.explanation: Sir Jim Ratcliffe of the chemicals firm INEOS, a boyhood United fan. He cut costs, cut staff and cut the free lunches, and results did not improve.
questions.why: Ratcliffe is the 2024 chapter in the who's-to-blame saga. Fans have strong views.
questions.use: Ask him: "Has Ratcliffe made anything better, honestly?"

questions.question: Manchester United won the 2024 FA Cup by beating which club?
questions.explanation: Manchester City, 2-1 at Wembley, as heavy underdogs, denying City a second double in a row. The manager was sacked months later anyway.
questions.why: Beating City in a final is the happiest recent United memory. Bring it up on a bad day.
questions.use: "They beat City in the 2024 cup final and sacked the manager anyway. Only United."

questions.question: What is Newcastle United's home ground called?
questions.explanation: St James' Park, right in the middle of the city since 1892. You can see the stands from the shopping streets.
questions.why: A stadium in the city centre is part of why Newcastle feels like a football city.
questions.use: "St James' is right in the middle of town. Walk from the shops to the match."

questions.question: What colours are Newcastle's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Black and white stripes since 1894, hence the Magpies. Sunderland, the rivals, wear red and white stripes.
questions.why: Two striped teams, one rivalry. Getting the colours right is the minimum.
questions.use: "Black and white is Newcastle. Red and white is Sunderland. Don't confuse them in the North East."

questions.question: What is Newcastle United's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Magpies, for the stripes. The fans are the Toon Army; Toon is how Geordies say town.
questions.why: 'The Toon' is how he refers to Newcastle. It means town in the local accent.
questions.use: "Howay the Toon. It just means 'come on Newcastle'."

questions.question: Who are Newcastle's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Sunderland, twelve miles down the road, in the Tyne-Wear derby. Two rivers, two cities, over a century of not getting on. Newcastle fans call Sunderland fans Mackems.
questions.why: The North East derby is as fierce as any in England. Know the names both sides use.
questions.use: "Tyne-Wear derby. Geordies against Mackems. Properly nasty."

questions.question: Who is Newcastle United's top scorer in the club's history?
questions.explanation: Alan Shearer, 206 goals, a Geordie who turned down Manchester United in 1996 to come home. His statue stands outside the ground, arm raised in his goal celebration.
questions.why: Shearer is Newcastle. If you know one player, know him.
questions.use: "Shearer turned down United to come home. That's why they worship him."

questions.question: Newcastle paid a world-record fee for Alan Shearer in 1996. How much?
questions.explanation: £15 million, from Blackburn Rovers, the biggest fee ever paid for a footballer at the time. Fifteen thousand fans turned up just to watch him hold up a shirt.
questions.why: A world record for a local boy coming home is a story the whole city shares.
questions.use: "Shearer cost fifteen million in 1996, a world record. Fifteen thousand people came to see him hold up a shirt."

questions.question: Where did Kevin Keegan's Entertainers finish in 1996 after leading the league by twelve points?
questions.explanation: Second, behind Manchester United, having been twelve points clear in January. The best-loved team to win nothing, and fans have not fully recovered.
questions.why: 'The Entertainers' is the phrase for that team. The collapse is the club's great what-if.
questions.use: Ask him: "Do Newcastle fans forgive Keegan for 1996, or do they love him anyway?"

questions.question: In which year was Newcastle United bought by a Saudi-led consortium?
questions.explanation: 2021, ending Mike Ashley's fourteen unloved years as owner. Fans celebrated outside the ground, some in Saudi dress, which caused a row of its own.
questions.why: The takeover is the dividing line in modern Newcastle. Before and after.
questions.use: Ask him: "Do you feel OK about where the money comes from, or do you not think about it?"

questions.question: Before 2025, in which year had Newcastle won a domestic trophy?
questions.explanation: 1955, the FA Cup, their third in five years. Then seventy years of nothing, which became the club's identity.
questions.why: Seventy years without a trophy is the number that explains the tears in 2025.
questions.use: "Seventy years between domestic trophies. 1955 to 2025. That's why grown men cried at Wembley."

questions.question: Newcastle won the League Cup in 2025 by beating which club?
questions.explanation: Liverpool, 2-1 at Wembley. Dan Burn, a six-foot-seven Geordie who had grown up a fan, scored the first goal. The city did not sleep.
questions.why: The 2025 cup is the happiest day in the life of every Newcastle fan under seventy. Ask about it.
questions.use: Ask him: "Where were you when Newcastle won the cup? Did you cry? Be honest."

questions.question: In which year did Newcastle win their fourth league title?
questions.explanation: 1927. Four titles, all before the Second World War. They have finished second four times since and no higher.
questions.why: The fourth title being before the war explains the yearning.
questions.use: "Four titles, and the fourth was 1927. Before anyone alive was born."

questions.question: What is the name of the stand at the south end of St James' Park where the loudest fans gather?
questions.explanation: The Gallowgate End, named after the road that led to the old town gallows. Where the songs start.
questions.why: A stand named after a road to the gallows is a fact with atmosphere.
questions.use: "The Gallowgate End is named after the road to the old gallows. Cheerful."

questions.question: Which manager, later knighted, managed Newcastle from 1999 to 2004 and was a Geordie himself?
questions.explanation: Sir Bobby Robson, born in County Durham, who took Newcastle into the Champions League in his late sixties. Sacked at 71, adored forever. His statue is outside the ground.
questions.why: Robson is the grandfather figure of the club. Speaking of him warmly is always right.
questions.use: "Bobby Robson got them into the Champions League at seventy. And they sacked him."

questions.question: Which manager took Newcastle back into the Champions League in 2023?
questions.explanation: Eddie Howe, appointed in 2021 with the club in the relegation zone. Fourth place eighteen months later, and the 2025 League Cup after that.
questions.why: Howe is the man who turned the money into football. Fans say his name with relief.
questions.use: "Howe took them from the relegation zone to the Champions League in eighteen months."

questions.question: Kevin Keegan's 1996 TV rant, 'I would love it if we beat them', was aimed at which manager?
questions.explanation: Alex Ferguson, who had suggested teams tried harder against United than Newcastle. Keegan, in headphones, lost it live on television. Newcastle lost the title anyway.
questions.why: 'I would love it' is one of football's best-known clips. Know the story behind it.
questions.use: "'I would love it if we beat them. Love it.' Keegan, 1996, live on Sky, in headphones. They didn't."

questions.question: Which retail billionaire owned Newcastle from 2007 to 2021?
questions.explanation: Mike Ashley of Sports Direct, who renamed the stadium after his shop, sold the best players and was protested against for fourteen years.
questions.why: The Ashley years are the misery the takeover ended. He is the villain of every fan's story.
questions.use: Ask him: "How bad were the Ashley years, honestly?"

questions.question: Newcastle United were formed in 1892 by the merger of which two clubs?
options: Newcastle East End and West End
questions.explanation: Newcastle East End and Newcastle West End. East End moved into West End's ground, St James' Park, and the merged club took a new name.
questions.why: Two clubs became one on the same pitch they play on today. Neat.
questions.use: "Newcastle are two clubs merged, East End and West End. Same ground since 1892."

questions.question: Newcastle sits on which river?
questions.explanation: The Tyne, with its famous bridges. Sunderland sits on the Wear twelve miles south, hence the Tyne-Wear derby.
questions.why: Rivers name the derby. Two rivers, two clubs.
questions.use: "Tyne's Newcastle, Wear's Sunderland. That's the derby's name sorted."

questions.question: Which European trophy did Newcastle win in 1969?
questions.explanation: The Inter-Cities Fairs Cup, forerunner of the UEFA Cup, beating Újpest of Hungary over two legs. Their one European trophy.
questions.why: A European trophy few people remember is the perfect impress fact.
questions.use: "Newcastle won a European trophy in 1969. The Fairs Cup. Nobody outside Newcastle remembers."

questions.question: Alexander Isak joined Newcastle in 2022 from which club?
questions.explanation: Real Sociedad, for around £60 million, a club record at the time. The Swede scored the goals that won the cup, then left for Liverpool in 2025 in a bitter summer.
questions.why: Isak's exit is the fresh wound. Approach with care.
questions.use: Ask him: "Isak to Liverpool. Betrayal, or just business?"

questions.question: What is Nottingham Forest's home ground called?
questions.explanation: The City Ground, on the south bank of the River Trent since 1898. Notts County's ground is 300 yards away across the river, the closest two league grounds in England.
questions.why: Two grounds you can see from each other is a fact people refuse to believe.
questions.use: "Forest and Notts County's grounds are three hundred yards apart. Either side of the river."

questions.question: What colour are Nottingham Forest's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Red, known as Garibaldi red after the Italian revolutionary whose followers wore it. Forest chose it in 1865, and gave a set of shirts to Arsenal when they were founded.
questions.why: Arsenal wear red because Forest sent them shirts. A genuinely good fact.
questions.use: "Arsenal play in red because Forest gave them their first kit in 1886."

questions.question: How many times have Nottingham Forest won the European Cup?
questions.explanation: Twice, in 1979 and 1980, back to back, having been promoted to the top flight in 1977. No club of that size has done anything like it.
questions.why: Two European Cups for a provincial club is the fact that makes Forest special. Fans live on it.
questions.use: "Two European Cups. Back to back. Two years after getting promoted."

questions.question: Which manager led Nottingham Forest to their European Cups?
questions.explanation: Brian Clough, the best-quoted manager in English football: 'I wouldn't say I was the best in the business, but I was in the top one.' His statue is in the city centre.
questions.why: Clough quotes are a genre. Knowing the man behind them is the point.
questions.use: Ask him: "What's your favourite Clough quote?" He has one.

questions.question: Between which years did Brian Clough manage Nottingham Forest?
questions.explanation: 1975 to 1993, eighteen years. He took them from the second division to European champions in four seasons, and retired after relegation in his final year.
questions.why: The Clough years are the club's whole identity. Dates help you place the stories.
questions.use: "Clough was there eighteen years. Second division to European champions in four."

questions.question: Who did Forest beat in the 1979 European Cup final?
questions.explanation: Malmö of Sweden, 1-0 in Munich, with a diving header from Trevor Francis, the first player ever to cost a million pounds.
questions.why: The million-pound man scoring the winner is the tidy detail.
questions.use: "The first million-pound footballer scored Forest's European Cup winner. Trevor Francis, 1979."

questions.question: Trevor Francis, the 1979 European Cup final scorer, was the first British player to cost how much?
questions.explanation: One million pounds, from Birmingham City in 1979. Clough claimed the fee was £999,999 so it would not go to the player's head, then made him make the tea.
questions.why: Clough making a million-pound signing make tea is the Clough story to tell.
questions.use: "Clough paid a million for Trevor Francis, then made him make the tea for the other players."

questions.question: Who did Forest beat in the 1980 European Cup final?
questions.explanation: Hamburg, 1-0 in Madrid, with Kevin Keegan in the German side. John Robertson, a chain-smoking Scottish winger, scored the goal.
questions.why: Two finals, two 1-0 wins. Forest fans know both scorers by heart.
questions.use: "Robertson scored in 1980. Clough said he was a genius with a fag in his mouth."

questions.question: Who are Nottingham Forest's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Derby County, fifteen miles away. Clough managed both clubs and won the league with both, which made the rivalry worse. Their matches are for the Brian Clough Trophy.
questions.why: A rivalry where both sides claim the same hero is unusual. This is it.
questions.use: "Forest and Derby both claim Clough. He won the league with both. They play for a trophy named after him."

questions.question: When Forest returned to the Premier League in 2022, how many years had they been away?
questions.explanation: Twenty-three years, since relegation in 1999, including three seasons in the third tier. Fans of a European champion, watching League One.
questions.why: Twenty-three years away is the context for how emotional the return was.
questions.use: Ask him: "Twenty-three years out of the Premier League. Did you keep going through the third division?"

questions.question: Which Welsh manager took Nottingham Forest back to the Premier League in 2022?
questions.explanation: Steve Cooper, who took over with Forest bottom of the Championship in September and won the play-off final at Wembley in May. Fans put his face on flags.
questions.why: Bottom in September to promoted in May is the turnaround fans measure others against.
questions.use: "Cooper took Forest from bottom of the Championship to promoted in one season."

questions.question: In which year was Nottingham Forest founded?
questions.explanation: 1865, by a group of shinty players, at a meeting in a pub. Among the oldest clubs in the world, and the first to use shin pads.
questions.why: Forest invented shin pads. A fact that works on anyone who has ever played.
questions.use: "Forest invented shin pads. 1874. A player cut down his cricket pads."

questions.question: In which year did Nottingham Forest win the league title?
questions.explanation: 1978, the season after promotion, and a year before the first European Cup. Their one title, the first of Clough's miracles.
questions.why: Winning the league the year after promotion is the beginning of the Forest legend.
questions.use: "They won the league the season after coming up. Then two European Cups. In three years."

questions.question: Which Forest goalkeeper of the European Cup years went on to 125 England caps?
questions.explanation: Peter Shilton, 125 caps, a figure no outfield player had reached by 2024. He played professionally until he was 47.
questions.why: The keeper who played until 47 is a fact for anyone who feels old.
questions.use: "Forest's keeper Peter Shilton played until he was 47. Forty-seven."

questions.question: Which England defender, nicknamed Psycho, captained Forest for over a decade?
questions.explanation: Stuart Pearce, a former electrician who kept advertising his trade in the match programme in case anyone needed a job doing. Famous for his 1996 penalty roar for England.
questions.why: Pearce is the hard man fans of every club respect. The electrician detail seals it.
questions.use: "Pearce kept advertising as an electrician in the programme while captaining Forest and England."

questions.question: Which Greek shipping magnate has owned Nottingham Forest since 2017?
questions.explanation: Evangelos Marinakis, who also owns Olympiacos in Greece. Volatile, generous, and once ran onto the pitch to argue with his own manager.
questions.why: Owners are a topic at every club now. Forest's is one of the more colourful.
questions.use: Ask him: "Is Marinakis good for Forest, or one bad month from chaos?"

questions.question: What is Nottingham Forest's mascot called?
questions.explanation: Sherwood the Bear. Robin Hood's forest, a bear. The logic is not explained further.
questions.why: Mascot names are the safest small talk in football.
questions.use: "Sherwood the Bear. There are no bears in Sherwood Forest, but fine."

questions.question: What is the name of the stand behind the goal at the City Ground where the home fans gather?
questions.explanation: The Trent End, backing onto the river. Clough called the fans there the twelfth man.
questions.why: Stands with names are stands with reputations. The Trent End is Forest's.
questions.use: "The Trent End. Right on the river."

questions.question: The trophy contested between Forest and Derby County is named after whom?
questions.explanation: Brian Clough, who won the league with both clubs. The trophy began in 2007, three years after his death, and the two sets of fans argue over which club he loved more.
questions.why: Two rivals sharing a hero is a rare thing in football.
questions.use: Ask him: "Was Clough more Forest or more Derby, really?"

questions.question: Nottingham Forest are from which county?
questions.explanation: Nottinghamshire, in the East Midlands. Derby and Leicester, the rivals, are the neighbouring counties.
questions.why: The East Midlands triangle explains the rivalries in one map.
questions.use: "Nottingham, Derby and Leicester. Three cities in a triangle, all hate each other."

questions.question: What is Tottenham Hotspur's home ground called?
questions.explanation: The Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, opened in 2019 on the site of the old White Hart Lane, with a pitch that slides away for American football games and a cheese room.
questions.why: The new stadium is the club's proudest possession. Praise it and he glows.
questions.use: "The new stadium's ridiculous. There's a cheese room. And the pitch slides out for the NFL."

questions.question: What was the name of Spurs' old ground, demolished in 2017?
questions.explanation: White Hart Lane, their home from 1899. The new stadium was built around it and over it; fans call the new place the Lane too, out of habit.
questions.why: 'The Lane' is what he calls home. Old ground or new.
questions.use: "Are you going to the Lane on Saturday?"

questions.question: What colours are Spurs' home kit?
questions.explanation: White shirts, navy shorts. The Lilywhites, an old nickname nobody under sixty uses.
questions.why: Kit recognition is how you follow a match without commentary.
questions.use: "White shirts, navy shorts. Spurs."

questions.question: Who are Tottenham's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Arsenal, since 1913, when Arsenal moved to north London four miles from Spurs, uninvited. Spurs fans resent that, and the 1919 vote that lifted Arsenal over them.
questions.why: The Arsenal grievance has two parts, and the 1919 one is the bit few people know.
questions.use: "Spurs hate Arsenal partly for moving in next door in 1913 and partly for a dodgy vote in 1919 that put Arsenal up instead of them."

questions.question: Spurs won the Europa League in 2025 by beating which club in the final?
questions.explanation: Manchester United, 1-0 in Bilbao, in a season where Spurs finished 17th in the league. Their first trophy in seventeen years, and a Champions League place.
questions.why: The 2025 trophy ended seventeen years of jokes. He will want to relive it.
questions.use: Ask him: "Bilbao 2025. Where were you when the whistle went?"

questions.question: Which Australian manager led Spurs to the 2025 Europa League?
questions.explanation: Ange Postecoglou, who had said 'I always win something in my second season' and was mocked for it until he did. He was sacked sixteen days after the final.
questions.why: Winning a trophy and being sacked a fortnight later is peak Spurs. He will have a view.
questions.use: Ask him: "Sacking Ange two weeks after he won you a trophy. Right call or madness?"

questions.question: Before 2025, in which year had Spurs won a trophy?
questions.explanation: 2008, the League Cup, beating Chelsea 2-1 at Wembley. Seventeen years of jokes followed, including a whole genre about Spurs bottling things.
questions.why: 'Spursy' became an adjective in those years. Knowing why is knowing the club's self-image.
questions.use: "Seventeen years without a trophy. 'Spursy' became an actual word."

questions.question: Who is Tottenham's top scorer in the club's history?
questions.explanation: Harry Kane, 280 goals, passing Jimmy Greaves in 2023 before leaving for Bayern Munich. A local boy who came through the academy.
questions.why: Kane is the club's modern hero and its great what-if. Both at once.
questions.use: Ask him: "Do you wish Kane had stayed, or was leaving the right thing for him?"

questions.question: Harry Kane left Spurs in 2023 to join which club?
questions.explanation: Bayern Munich, for around £100 million, chasing a trophy. Bayern then failed to win the league for the first time in eleven years. He got his medal in 2025.
questions.why: The Kane trophy curse was a running joke across football for two years.
questions.use: "Kane went to Bayern for a trophy and they immediately stopped winning. Then he finally got one."

questions.question: Which manager led Spurs to the league and cup double in 1961?
questions.explanation: Bill Nicholson, the club's greatest manager, whose team won the first double of the twentieth century. The road outside the stadium is named after him.
questions.why: The 1961 double is the club's high point. Older fans measure everything against it.
questions.use: "1961 double. Bill Nicholson. The road outside the ground is named after him."

questions.question: In 1963 Spurs became the first British club to win a European trophy. Which?
questions.explanation: The Cup Winners' Cup, beating Atlético Madrid 5-1 in Rotterdam. Jimmy Greaves scored twice. A British first.
questions.why: Being first in Europe is a fact Spurs fans hold onto when the trophy count is mentioned.
questions.use: "Spurs were the first British club to win in Europe. 1963, beat Atlético 5-1."

questions.question: Whose club goalscoring mark did Harry Kane pass in 2023?
questions.explanation: Jimmy Greaves, whose 266 goals had stood since 1970. Greaves was the great goalscorer of his era, and later a much-loved TV presenter.
questions.why: Greaves is the name older fans use to explain what a striker should be.
questions.use: "Greaves scored 266 for Spurs and was on telly for years after. Kane finally passed him."

questions.question: Gareth Bale left Spurs in 2013 for a world-record fee to join which club?
questions.explanation: Real Madrid, for about £85 million. He won five Champions Leagues there, scored in two finals, and came back to Spurs on loan for a farewell.
questions.why: Bale is the Spurs player who went and won everything elsewhere. It stings and it doesn't.
questions.use: Ask him: "Bale winning five Champions Leagues at Madrid. Proud or gutted?"

questions.question: Spurs reached the Champions League final in 2019 and lost to which club?
questions.explanation: Liverpool, 2-0 in Madrid, after a penalty in the second minute. The semi-final comeback against Ajax, three second-half goals away from home, was the night fans remember.
questions.why: The Ajax semi is the greatest Spurs night of the century. The final is the footnote.
questions.use: Ask him: "The Ajax semi-final. Lucas Moura's third goal. Where were you?"

questions.question: Which Argentine managed Spurs from 2014 to 2019 and took them to that Champions League final?
questions.explanation: Mauricio Pochettino, adored by the fans, who built the best Spurs team in decades on a small budget and was sacked five months after the final.
questions.why: Pochettino is the manager Spurs fans pine for. Say his name and watch.
questions.use: "Poch. Best they've had in my lifetime, he'll say. Then they sacked him."

questions.question: The cockerel on the Spurs badge stands on what?
questions.explanation: A football. The cockerel has been on the badge since 1909 and wears spurs on its legs, which is the pun: Hotspur, spurs.
questions.why: He has looked at that badge a thousand times and may not have noticed the spurs.
questions.use: Ask him: "Did you know the cockerel on the badge is wearing spurs? That's the joke."

questions.question: What is Tottenham Hotspur's Latin motto?
questions.explanation: Audere est Facere: to dare is to do. It is on the badge and, after the 2025 final, on a lot of tattoos.
questions.why: 'To dare is to do' is the phrase Spurs fans quote in hope and in irony.
questions.use: "To dare is to do. That's the motto. They dared a lot and did very little for seventeen years."

questions.question: Tottenham Hotspur are named after which historical figure?
questions.explanation: Harry Hotspur, a medieval knight whose family owned land in the area, and a character in Shakespeare's Henry IV. Schoolboys chose the name in 1882.
questions.why: A club named after a Shakespeare character is a good fact for a non-football crowd too.
questions.use: "Spurs are named after a Shakespeare character. Harry Hotspur, from Henry IV."

questions.question: Spurs are from which part of London?
questions.explanation: North London, in Tottenham, a few miles from Arsenal. Both clubs claim to be the real north London club.
questions.why: Two clubs, one postcode area, one argument about who belongs.
questions.use: "North London's ours, he'll say. Arsenal fans say the same. Neither will budge."

questions.question: Which American sport is played every year at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium?
questions.explanation: American football, the NFL. The stadium has a second artificial pitch under the grass one; the grass slides out in sections for the games.
questions.why: The sliding pitch is the fact that impresses people who don't care about football at all.
questions.use: "The Spurs pitch slides out in three pieces so the NFL can play on the one underneath."

questions.question: What is Sunderland's home ground called?
questions.explanation: The Stadium of Light, since 1997, built on the site of a coal mine. The name honours the miners' lamps, and a Davy lamp stands outside.
questions.why: The coal mine is the story. Benfica's stadium has the same name, which confuses people.
questions.use: "It's built on an old pit. The Stadium of Light is for the miners' lamps."

questions.question: What is Sunderland's nickname?
questions.explanation: The Black Cats, chosen by fans in a vote in 2000. A black cat was the lucky mascot at the 1937 cup final. Newcastle fans call them Mackems, which is not affectionate.
questions.why: Two names: the one they chose and the one their rivals use.
questions.use: "Black Cats officially. Mackems if you're from Newcastle and being rude."

questions.question: What colours are Sunderland's home shirts?
questions.explanation: Red and white stripes with black shorts. Newcastle wear black and white; do not mix them up within fifty miles of either city.
questions.why: In the North East, stripe colour is identity.
questions.use: "Red and white stripes. Not black and white. Very important distinction up there."

questions.question: Who are Sunderland's fiercest rivals?
questions.explanation: Newcastle United, twelve miles north, in the Tyne-Wear derby. Two rivers, two cities, total mutual dislike. Newcastle fans are Geordies; Sunderland fans are Mackems.
questions.why: The derby is the fixture that decides his year. Know the date.
questions.use: Ask him: "When's the derby? Are we hiding the sharp objects?"

questions.question: What was Sunderland's home ground before 1997?
questions.explanation: Roker Park, their home from 1898, famous for the Roker Roar, a noise visiting teams dreaded. Fans use the phrase for the club's atmosphere to this day.
questions.why: 'The Roker Roar' is a phrase he may use. It survived the ground.
questions.use: "The Roker Roar. The old ground's gone but they kept the name for the noise."

questions.question: In which year was Sunderland founded?
questions.explanation: 1879, by a schoolteacher, as Sunderland and District Teachers' Association Football Club. The teachers part went within a year.
questions.why: A club founded by teachers is a gentle origin story for a fierce fanbase.
questions.use: "Sunderland were founded by schoolteachers. It was a teachers' association club for a year."

questions.question: How many league titles have Sunderland won?
questions.explanation: Six, all between 1892 and 1936. In the 1890s they were called the Team of All Talents, the best in England.
questions.why: Six titles puts Sunderland among the big historic clubs, which surprises people who only know recent years.
questions.use: "Sunderland have six league titles. More than Chelsea had until 2017. All before the war, mind."

questions.question: Sunderland, then in the second division, won the 1973 FA Cup by beating which club?
questions.explanation: Leeds United, the best team in England at the time, 1-0 at Wembley. One of the great cup shocks, and the club's defining moment.
questions.why: 1973 is the story every Sunderland fan's parents told them. It is the founding myth.
questions.use: Ask him: "Was anyone in your family at Wembley in 1973?"

questions.question: Who scored the winning goal in the 1973 FA Cup final?
questions.explanation: Ian Porterfield, in the first half. Then goalkeeper Jim Montgomery made a double save so good people argue to this day whether it was the best ever.
questions.why: The Montgomery save is the moment fans replay in their heads. Name it and he'll finish the story.
questions.use: "Porterfield scored, but it's the Montgomery double save everyone talks about."

questions.question: Which Sunderland manager ran across Wembley in a raincoat and trilby to hug his goalkeeper in 1973?
questions.explanation: Bob Stokoe. The run is a statue outside the Stadium of Light, arms out, hat on. Fans meet there before games.
questions.why: The statue is a landmark. Knowing what it shows makes you part of the story.
questions.use: "The statue outside the ground is the manager running to hug his keeper after the 1973 final. Raincoat and all."

questions.question: Sunderland dropped to League One in 2018. In which year did they return to the Championship?
questions.explanation: 2022, after four seasons in the third tier, via the play-off final against Wycombe. Two of those seasons produced a Netflix series.
questions.why: The League One years are the trauma. Knowing how long they lasted shows you understand.
questions.use: Ask him: "Four years in League One. Did you keep your season ticket?"

questions.question: What was the name of the Netflix documentary series about Sunderland's decline?
questions.explanation: Sunderland 'Til I Die, three series of things going wrong, watched all over the world. Fans did not enjoy being famous for misery.
questions.why: It is the one Sunderland reference non-fans know. Use it carefully.
questions.use: Ask him: "Did you watch the Netflix series, or was it too painful?"

questions.question: Sunderland were promoted to the Premier League in 2025 by beating which club in the play-off final?
questions.explanation: Sheffield United, 2-1 at Wembley, with a winner in the 95th minute from Tom Watson, a teenager who had already agreed to join Brighton.
questions.why: A 95th-minute winner from a kid on his way out is the kind of ending fans cannot believe happened to them.
questions.use: "Sunderland went up with a 95th-minute winner from a teenager who'd already signed for Brighton."

questions.question: Which French manager led Sunderland to promotion in 2025?
questions.explanation: Régis Le Bris, in his first season, barely known in England when he arrived. Quiet, and the fans took to him immediately.
questions.why: Le Bris is the name on the promotion. The fans' respect for him is total.
questions.use: "Le Bris. Nobody had heard of him. Took them up in his first season."

questions.question: Which former Sunderland striker, from Ireland, later became the club's chairman?
questions.explanation: Niall Quinn, who led an Irish takeover in 2006 and hired Roy Keane as manager. He also gave his testimonial money to charity and once paid for stranded fans' taxis home.
questions.why: The player who paid for fans' taxis is why Quinn is loved on Wearside.
questions.use: "Niall Quinn once paid for taxis for a hundred stranded Sunderland fans. Then became chairman."

questions.question: Which Sunderland striker won the European Golden Shoe in 2000 with 30 Premier League goals?
questions.explanation: Kevin Phillips, the one Englishman to win Europe's top-scorer award by 2024. He had been playing non-league football six years earlier.
questions.why: An Englishman winning the Golden Shoe is rare. Sunderland fans know who it was.
questions.use: "Kevin Phillips out-scored everyone in Europe in 2000. From non-league to Golden Shoe in six years."

questions.question: Sunderland sits on which river?
questions.explanation: The Wear. The Stadium of Light sits on its north bank, opposite the old shipyards.
questions.why: River names name the derby. Wear is Sunderland.
questions.use: "The Wear. Newcastle's the Tyne. Hence Tyne-Wear."

questions.question: What are Sunderland's two black cat mascots called?
questions.explanation: Samson and Delilah. Samson has been at the club since 2000, the year the fans voted for the Black Cats name.
questions.why: Biblical mascots are a fact that raises a smile in a quiet moment.
questions.use: "Samson and Delilah. The mascots. Very Old Testament."

questions.question: Which England goalkeeper came through Sunderland's academy before joining Everton in 2017?
questions.explanation: Jordan Pickford, born in Washington, Tyne and Wear. Sunderland got £25 million for him, then a world record for a British goalkeeper.
questions.why: The England keeper is a Sunderland lad. Good to have when he is on screen.
questions.use: "Pickford's a Sunderland boy. Came through their academy."

questions.question: Which England midfielder and Liverpool captain also came through Sunderland's academy?
questions.explanation: Jordan Henderson, born in Sunderland, who left for Liverpool in 2011 and lifted the Champions League and the league as captain.
questions.why: Two England players from one academy in a few years is a point of pride.
questions.use: "Henderson and Pickford both came through Sunderland's academy. Two England regulars."
